abner-debleu-chinook-1903-07-31.A1: SHIPPED TO ASTORIA -The peace and quiet of that sequestered little nook called Chinook was rudely disturbed yesterday by a member of the Afro-American race, and for about ten minutes it was a question whether there would be a lynching or just plain tar and feathers. The name of the black contention is Abner Debleu, and the offense charged against him was just plain laziness. The people of Chinook offered him work, which he declined, preferring to bask in the warm sunshine by day and beg, borrow or steal his food by night. Then the citizens got together and decided that they had no room in their clean little town for such a man, and he was told to "get." Again he refused, and the trouble began. In order to avert trouble the men folks took up a collection to raise funds to send him away. They gathered a small handful of silver, amounting to $2.75. Jack Johnson happened to be in town and not wishing to officiate at a lynching, he took the colored gentleman abord the steamer Miller and brought him to Astoria, where he was
abner-debleu-chinook-1903-07-31.A2: turned over to Chief of Police Hallock, along with the $2.75 collected. Chief Hallock knew the chocolate colored gentleman the minute he set eyes on him. It seems that he honored the city with a visit during regatta several years ago, and that settled him as far as this city was concerned. He will be given the alternative of getting out of the city or going to jail.
abner-debleu-chinook-1903-07-31.A3: MR. ABNER DEBLEU LEAVES TOWN—The colored gentleman from Chinook who honored Astoria with a visit on Friday, reconsidered his former decision to remain here in spite of Chief Hallock's orders, and after languishing in the city tank all night and all day yesterday, accepted the $2.75 subscribed for him by the people of Chinook, and was escorted to the Portland boat last night. He was put aboard and an officer stood by the gang plank until the steamer put to sea, in order to be sure that the chicken chaser's mind did not undergo another change. Debleu was anxious to return to Chinook "jes to show them people as what I ain't a-skeered o' them" but again the good council of the chief prevailed, and before he left, he was convinced that Chinook was a bad place for lazy folks.
abner-debleu-chinook-1903-07-31.A4:
ABNER RETURNED TO CHINOOK
—Abner Debleu, the chocolate colored gentleman who occupied a cell at the police headquarters a few nights ago pending his decision to leave town, returned to Chinook, the puritan little Siwagh village on the river, from which he had been given a free pass out and a small purse to help him along his weary way. The people of Chinook vowed that they would soil the spotless white shield of their town if Abner persisted in intruding his presence on their streets. However, he returned for the purpose of "showing them there white trash that I se aint afraid o'em" and he passed through the town but did not
abner-debleu-chinook-1903-07-31.A5: tarry long enough to invite forcible measures of removal. Debleu is said to possess a wonderful knowledge of biblical history. He made Pasific county, Wash.,his hearquarters for many years and though of very youthful appearance is said to have passed the fortleth wilestone.

WHITE GIRL LIVING WITH NEGRO NEAR DOVER
Citizens Threatened Violence and Authorities Arrested the Couple
Special to the Evening Journal.

Dover, Dec. 22.—Sheriff Melvin, Constable Williams and Policemen Killen and Russell this morning surrounded a house at Puncheon Run and arrested there Bertie Fleming, a white girl of 20 years, who was living with a negro, Smith, 45 years old.

There had been threats of whitecapping the couple, but the authorities took time by the forelock and arrested the pair as suspicious characters, expecting to charge them with other crimes at the hearing before Magistrate Wood tomorrow.

bun-fender-1903-08-27.A1:
WHIPPED A NEGRO.
Woman's Screams Had Put Him to Flight.
Flight.

Tifton, Ga., Aug. 27.—Mrs. Bradshaw, a young white woman living near Fender, was horried on awaking last night to find a negro at her bedside. She gave the alarm, and the negro fled, but not before she recognized him, despite the dim light, as Bun, 15 years old, employed on the place. The men who came in response to her call were so close after the negro that he escaped without his clothes, but some time during the night he secured an old pair of trousers that were hanging in an outhouse.

Next morning the negro was followed, and captured about 11 o'clock. Several young men started to Tifton jail with him, but he escaped before they got there. Rumor says he escaped with one of the most thorough floggings that a boy of his size ever received, and was warned to leave the country and stay away.

NEWS OF THE DAY.
Ex-Lieut Gov. Tillman, who shot Editor Gonzales, is making no attempt to be released on bail. He prefers to stay in jail.

Governor Chamberlain, of Connecticut, has called out 12 companies of State troops to stop the rioting at Waterbury, caused by the trolley strike.

Treasury figures for 1902 show that exports of manufacturers increased $15,-500,000 and of agricultural products decreased $120,000,000, compared to 1901.

The Thomas Jefferson Memorial Association, through its president, Admiral Dewey, has issued an appeal for funds to build a memorial for Jefferson in Washington.

The new German tariff will inflict serious injury on the commerce of this country, barring important exports from the German market; the grin and flour exporting interests will suffer especially.

At the Indianapolis wage conference on Saturday, the operators unanimously voted not to grant the demand of the miners for higher wages and certain changes in the method of mining. The question was discussed and referred to the scale committee.

A dog supposed to be mad invaded the Waverly, Baltimore, Presbyterian church yesterday morning during the Sunday school services and bit a man, who proceeded to drive him out. Two boys were bitten on Saturday afternoon by a setter pup that had apparently been seized with rabies.

The Chesapeake and Ohio Canal boatmen at Williamsport, Md., announce their decision to reject the last proposition submitted the other day by Mr. G. L. Nicholson, general manager of the canal, according to which the transportation company agrees to pay 22 cents freight for hauling coal to that place, and 40 cents to Georgetown.

The Hill of Tara, so rich in historic memories, will shortly be sold at auction in Dublin. Until the sixth century Tara was the chief seat of the Irish kings. The last important gathering on the Hill of Tara was in 1843, when a gigantic meeting was held there under the auspices of Daniel O'Connell, who urged the repeal of the Union.

A black cat was found in an oats bin in a flour mill, near Manheim, Pa., on Saturday, in which she had been imprisoned for nearly a month. The cat had entered the partly-filled bin after a mouse and her movements had started the oats "running," which soon completely covered her. The cat was almost dead from her long fast.

Repeated attempts were made yesterday to lynch Charles Jefferson, a negro, who was lodged in jail at Washington, Pa., as the result of a criminal assault upon the 3-year-old daughter of Dr. George R. Conger, of that place. The little girl will die. At four different towns mobs were formed for the purpose of lynching the negro, but a strong body of constables succeeded in saving his life.

Cardinal Gibbons in his sermon on the divorce question in Baltimore said: "I can conceive of no more pathetic scenes, no appeal more touching, than the contemplation of a child emerging into the years of discretion seeing her father and mother estranged from each other. The nation is sick, and the malady is all the greater because the patient is unconscious of the disease.

Both Argentina and Chile have proposed to the United States the purchase of armored cruisers and battleships which they have under construction in Europe. In case of trouble between the United States and Germany, it is declared that these vessels will represent the balance of power, and it is therefore urged that the American Government should lose no time in acquiring them.

Rather than accept an assignment not to his liking, Naval Constructor Richmond Pearson Hobson has resigned from the navy. His resignation reached the Navy Department Saturday, and will be forwarded to the President in a few days with a recommendation that it be accepted. Mr. Hobson's letter accompanying his resignation is said to sizzle. He takes the position that he has been forced out of the navy. Mr. Hobson was assigned two weeks ago to take charge of the navy yard at Bremerton, Wash., and was directed to be there by February 9.

Three men were killed, four fatally injured, and ten seriously hurt in a rear end collision of two stock trains that took place on the Illinois Central, one mile west of Cloverdale, early this morning.

THE SAME EVERYWHERE.

On Sunday last the Rev. Dr. Charles H. Parkhurst, of New York, announced that at the Wednesday Evening Prayer Meeting there would be an address by a negro missionary, and in making the announcement said:

"Even at this day, so long after the proclamation of emancipation, there is in many parts of the South a condition of veritable slavery. Although we claim to be a civilized people, there is a degree of barbarism in our treatment of the black race that is not exceeded in any part of the world. And although we send out missionaries to Christianize other lands, there are communities in the South as un-Christian as any part of heathendom."

A Southerner who happened to be in the church at the time rose and politely informed Dr. Parkhurst that he was mistaken as to the situation in the South. The negroes were treated properly, he asserted, and no credence was to be given to the sensational reports of their systematic ill-treatment.

Dr. Parkhurst asked him about the "Grandfather Clause" in the Constitutions of some of the Southern States, and again asked him about lynchings, the Southerner making courteous replies, but standing up manfully for his people.

On that very day attempts were made in four different Pennsylvania towns to lynch a negro who had committed an assault upon a white child. The story is told by a correspondent of the Philadelphia Record, writing from Taylorstown, Pa. After the negro was captured and when the constable arrived to take him away a large crowd of people congregated, threatening vengeance. The constable secured a guard and started to the train with the negro, intending to bring him to the county jail at Taylorstown. The rest of the story is told by the correspondent. We quote:

"The officers with the prisoner in their midst, and with drawn revolvers, fought their way through the crowd and succeeded in getting their man aboard.

"At Clayville a mob of 300 men had gathered with a rope, determined to lynch the man, but the car doors were locked and an officer stood at each entrance with a revolver, and the crowd was cowed.

"Jefferson was taken off at Taylorstown in order that he might be identified. Here, also, the officers were compelled to fight their way through the crowd, and finally reached the Conger residence.

"As they entered the house Dr. Conger sprang in front of the negro with a drawn revolver and discharged the weapon at the cowering negro. An officer knocked his arm up and the shot whizzed through the air, within a few inches of Jefferson's face. Conger was then held until he identified the man, when he was again placed on board the train and brought here this evening.

"A crowd had gathered here, but there was no great demonstration, and the prisoner was safely landed in jail, followed up the streets by a hooting, threatening mob of people.

"The negro had to be carried the last few blocks, as he was completely overcome with terror. An extra guard has been placed on the jail here, as a demonstration by the residents of Taylorstown is expected."

We wonder if Dr. Parkhurst will refer to this incident at the prayer-meeting service this evening. Why did he not refer to the numerous race riots that have occurred in New York city within the past year or two? In some of these riots assaults were made upon negroes simply because they were negroes, and it was all the police could do to keep the blacks from being torn to pieces by the mob.

We do not justify or excuse lynching. We do not believe in mob law, but it arouses our indignation when Northern men try to make it appear that the South is worse in this respect than the North. There are more race clashes in the South than in the North for the reason that there are more negroes in the South, but wherever there is a large collection of negroes in any Northern community there the race question exists and there the bad negro is summarily punished by the indignant whites, whenever he goes on the rampage.

Dr. Parkhurst and those like him, who consider these facts, should also ask themselves the question why it is, if they are treated so much worse in the South than in the North, that the negroes do not pick themselves up in a body and move into Northern territory?

INTER-STATE COMMERCE COMMISSION FAVORED ELKINS REBATE BILL. Existing Law Does Not Provide For Punishment of a Railroad Itself. [Special Telegram to The Register.] WASHINGTON, Feb. 12.—The report on the Elkins rebate bill ordered favorably reported by the House committee on interstate commerce yesterday, was filed in the House today by Mr. Mann, of Illinois. "In extensive hearings before your committee upon the general subject of proposed amendments to the interstate commerce law," the report recites, "it was strongly urged by the members of the interstate commerce commission that the provisions of existing law providing for punishment of the officers and agents of railroads, but not for punishment of the railroad itself, prevented the enforcement of the law forbidding rebates and discriminations. [Special Telegram to The Register.] WASHINGTON, Pa., Feb. 12.—Intense excitement prevails over the case in court between Dr. George R. LYNCHING NEAR WARREN
Negro Rape Fiend Suffers the Usual Penalty For His Crime
Warten, Ark., July 20.—(Special.)—A lynching bee was pulled off near here Sunday night.

Saturday evening Crane Green, a negro employed at Childs' mill, nine miles northwest of Warren, committed an assault on a Miss Blake, the thirteen-year-old daughter of one of the white employees at the mill. The girl was considerably injured by the brute. Green made his escape, but the officers telephoned to every point in the county, and the people all over the county were on the lookout for Green. Sunday afternoon he was located at Lanark, and officers went to that place, arrested Green and started with him to this place to put him in jail. The officers who had Green in
crane-green-pine-bluff-1903-07-19.A2: charge have not arrived here yet, and it was not known until this morning why the officers had not put in their appearance with Green, when a farmer who came to the city reported that hanging to a limb on the Kingsland road, five miles north of Warren, was the body of a negro. Investigation the body of a negro. Investigation The lynchers did their work quietly. They went out on the Kingsland road and waited till the officers arrived with Green, took him from them, swung him up, and after being satisfied that Green was dead, quietly dispersed. It was not known here that Green had been lynched till the report was received here that his body was hanging from the limb of a tree in the roadside.
crane-green-pine-bluff-1903-07-19.A4:
LYNCHED NEGRO IN THE NIGHT.
Mob at Kingsland, Ark., Made No Demonstration.
REPUBLIC SPECIAL.

Pine Bluff, Ark., July 20.—Crane Green, a negro, was lynched quietly some time Sunday night about five miles from Kingsland on the Warren road. On Saturday afternoon he assaulted the 13-year-old daughter of William Blanke at Childs Mili, near Warren, and fled.

All the neighboring county was notified immediately and search was made. Green was located at Lanark, and Warren officers went after him. Nothing further was heard of Green until this morning, when a farmer came into Warren bringing the information that he saw Green's body hanging to a tree.

The identity of the lynchers is not known.

t NEGRO LYNCHED NEAR WARREN.
Committed Criminal Assault Upon Young White Girl, But Was Soon Captured By Mob and Strung Up to a Tree.
Warren, July 20.—On Saturday afternoon about 2 o'clock a negro named John Green entered the residence of W. E. Baker, a reputable white man employed at the Childs & Tracy mill, eight miles from town, and criminally assaulted his 14-year-old daughter. The mill was shut down for the day. A part of the force was in Warren and the remainder at religious service some distance from the mill. The girl was entirely alone, the only person on the mill premises being the watchman at the dry kilns, some distance off.

As soon as the facts became known parties of men started in pursuit of the negro. He was captured near Lanark yesterday morning. Word was received that he would be brought to town last night, but it was learned this morning that he was hanged by a mob last night about six miles from town, and within about two miles of the place where the crime was committed.

THE NEW YORK CABMEN. New Yorkers and visitors to New York have been long oppressed by cabmen. In spite of municipal regulations as to charges, the cabbies have managed to do about as they liked, relying in part on the weight of their own impudence and the disinclination of patrons to take the trouble to fight for their rights. Occasionally someone, like Mark Twain, has made things disagreeable for a cabman who has charged extortionate prices. But persons having sufficient public spirit to
go out of their way to bring the cabbies to terms have been rare.

Generally cabmen have fixed the tariff to suit themselves. But there has been a great deal of dissatisfaction and there have been many appeals to the authorities for better conditions. Now it is believed that the arbitrary rule of the cabman is part, for the corporation counsel interprets the new regulations relating to cabmen as meaning that cabmen must carry at prices legally specified. Hitherto the cabman has deemed it his right to make whatever demands he saw fit: His abuse of patrons took many forms and, not infrequently, when disputes arose, passengers were landed at police station. Henceforth, however, unless people permit themselves to be imposed upon without protest they can ride about New York without being mercilessly robbed.

Cabmen in large cities are likely to take all that they can get. In London the person who does not keep himself informed as to rates and distances may easily fall victim to the greed of an astute cabman, but, on the other hand, a person who looks out for himself a little by keeping informed can enter a cab in London and without any haggling whatever travel where he pleases at reasonable rates. Cabs should be as well regulated in New York and in other American cities as in London. Whatever the scale of prices is the cabman should be held to it strictly.

The Irish Land bill has passed the House of Commons, and there is now no obstacle to its enactment. Mr. Balfour, the premier, in expressing his approbation was careful to say that the Irish question would remain, though it would no longer be embittered by social wrongs engendered through the present relations of landlord and tenant. The home rule controversy will not be confused henceforth with another controversy and embarrassed by it. To underestimate the effect of the land bill is far better than to overestimate it in order to avoid the shock of disappointment, should the measure fail to prove entirely satisfactory. Yet there is, no doubt, great hope among both English and Irish that the land measure, by offering new and more favorable conditions of life, will clear the way to a happy adjustment of all disturbing questions.

Coney Island, it is said, is rapidly losing all signs of "toughness" and is assuming more and more the appearance of a clean and respectable seaside resort. Coney was not in the old days as bad as it was painted, but it contained "dives" and was a rendezvous for thieves and "crooks" who preyed on the unwary and unsophisticated. Formerly, when there was talk of reforming Coney Island, there was a protest that rigid enforcement of the law would kill the place. But, under the present active police administration, the only complaint seems to be that transportation facilities are not adequate to the demands of the people who wish to get to the seashore. The idea that vicious dens make a seaside resort or any other summer resort or playground attractive, is obsolete. What people wish is a place where they can go and seek innocent pleasures. The persons who went to Coney Island to see the Old Bowery when that was in full operation were few in proportion to those who went for the pleasures to be had on the beach.

King Edward in visiting Ireland shows again the motive that seems thus far to have inspired his rule. He is strongly for peace at home and abroad and believes that peace can often be attained and maintained by the exercise of thoughtfulness and tact. The entrance to Dublin was in every way satisfactory, illustrating as it did the good sense of the Irish people and the broadminded policy of the King.

When prices fall in Wall Street because railways lack business there will be reason to suppose that all is not well with the country. But when, as recently, prices fall while reports are coming in that the railway business is excellent and the outlook for plenty of work most hopeful, the reasonable conclusion is that the country is all right and that the sickness does not extend much beyond the narrow walls of stock exchanges.

EDITORIAL COMMENT

An interesting contribution to the discussion growing out of the custom of giving liquor to soldiers is made by Count von Haeseler, until lately commander of the sixteenth army corps in Germany, and one of Emperor William's military favorites.

The count is not one of those who believe that strong drink is necessary to make a good soldier, nor does he believe that alcoholic stimulation increases the powers of endurance or the fighting quality in soldiers. On the contrary, Count von Haeseler, after twenty-five years of total abstinence in the army, protests strongly against

the use of liquor by soldiers.—Chicago Record-Herald.

Gov. Durbin, of Indiana, found it necessary to take prompt action to protect the State from anarchy, a number of persons having yielded to the solicitation of outsiders and discharged from their employment those who had served in the recent disturbances at Evansville. The conspirators hoped that the result of their action would be to make young men fearful of joining the Guard, while many who were in it would get out at the earliest possible opportunity. After a consultation with certain of the military authorities and the Attorney-General, it was found that, according to an act of 1893 reorganizing the militia, it is a penal offence to discharge a National Guardsman because he has served the State.

The National Guard of every State should be protected by a similar enactment.—New York Evening Sun.

NEGRO RENTERS TERRORIZED.
During the past week all negro renters living on lands in the Tomberlin neighborhood, Lonoke county, were notified by nightriders to leave the country at once, and as a result thirty-five families have moved to more congenial districts. The expulsion of negro renters is supposed to have been occasioned by land owners recently raising rents from $4 and $5 to $6 and $7. This antagonized the white renters, and their sympathizers propose to reduce rentals by causing shortage of renters.

WHITECAPPERS AGAIN.
Jackson, June 2.—News has just reached here of a recurrence of the whitecapping outrages in Franklin and Amite counties, and it seems that the stern treatment dealt out to previous offenders by the circuit courts has not had a permanent effect.

In Franklin county a negro named Dillon, living in the McCall Creek neighborhood, was visited by the whitecaps Saturday night, and fifty shots were fired into the house2. The inmates had narrow escapes from being killed. Dillon was warned about three weeks ago to leave the neighborhood and failed to do so.

In Amite county the whitecaps visited a negro on the Wilson place with the intention of giving him a thrashing, but the negro proved to be too strong for his assaliants. He wrenched himself from their grasp and started to run, when one of the party fired on him, and seven buckshot took lodgment in the negro's leg, and a pistol ball cut across his chin.

event-1903-06-4.A5:
WHITECAPS REAP WHIRLWIND.
The people of Franklin county, who have been engaging in the whitecapper outrages for the past year or so, are now reaping the fruits of their folly. A new farming season is at hand, and it is impossible to induce Negro laborers to go to that section for love or money. Fancy wages are being offered to induce Negro immigration to Franklin county, but without any degree of successful result. The consequence will be thousands of untitled acres in the county during the coming year and a long train of evils are following in the wake of the lawless conduct that has been carried on by white men under the gulse of enforcing law and order.

In Amite county and some sections of Lincoln the situation is equally as bad. The Negroes have steadily drifted out of the three counties, going to the cano fields of Louisiana, the rich plantations of the delta or the saw mills of south Mississippi, until today the three counties lack at least 80 per cent of the labor they need to properly till the soil and raise the usual crops.

THE POPE IS DEAD AMIO SHOWERS OF BULLETS FLEEING NEGRO MADE ESCAPE WILLIAM VINSON, A CATLETTSBURG YOUNG MAN, PROBABLY FA- TALLY STABBED BY NEGRO SATURDAY NIGHT;—NEGRO WAS CAPTURED IN OHIO.
William Vinson, a young man of Catlettsburg, was stabbed and probably fatally wounded by Gus Epps, a negro, in the alley on Eighth street between Second and Third avenue, Saturday night about half-past one o'clock. The cutting seems to have been entirely without provocation and the wounded man had not even spoken to the negro before the affair. Epps, after he had stabbed Vinson ran up Eighth street toward the C. & O. track and was not seen again until about half-past five o'clock Sunday morning when he was found in Camden park by a posse in this city who had gone in search of him.

The negro was shot at several times in the park and it is thought that he was wounded but he ran to Twelve-pole creek and procuring a boat escaped to the other side. The park and surrounding country was scoured by the party in search of the negro but he was not found.

When news of the affair reached Catlettsburg, Vinson's home, a searching party was at once organized and a thorough search made along the Camden Interstate car line from Catlettsburg to Camden park. When the negro was not found, the party went over into Ohio.

Vinson, the wounded man was taken to his home in Catlettsburg on the half past ten o'clock car Sunday morning. His condition this morning was reported as favorable and it is thought now that he will probably recover.

The cutting was witnessed by several friends of Vinson but it was not known at the time that he had been cut, the other young men thinking that he had only been hit. When he cried cut, "I am cut," his friends immediately gave chase to the negro who had run up Eighth street toward Third avenue. The negro escaped although he was followed for some distance by the young men and Lieutenant Sam Davis, who had been informed of the affair.

Vinson was taken to the office of Drs. Hogg; and Enslow where his wound was dressed and where he remained until Sunday morning when his mother and other relatives arrived from Catlettsburg.

Vinson's wound is a cut, probably made by a hooked blade knife, about two inches long, just over his right lung. It is very fortunate for him that the wound is on that side as the same cut on the left side of his breast would have been directly over his heart.

A posse composed of about twenty, young men, well armed, left on the five o'clock car for Kenova, where they thought that Epps might be found attempting to board a train for Columbus, Ohio.

As the car passed Camden park several of the party who knew Epps recognized him standing in a field near the car line. The car was stopped and the party got off and gave chase to the negro who, having seen them, was running towards Twelve Pole creek.

It is estimated that no less than fifty shots were fired at Epps, as he retreated into the bushes, and it is thought from his actions that he was wounded. He fell several times but at last reached the creek and jumping into a boat crossed to the other side out of range of the pistol shots. The posse then crossed on the trestle to the other side, but nothing more was seen of the negro and the hunt was finally given up. However the news of the affair had reached Catlettsburg and a party from that place was organized and a diligent search made for the negro. When nothing was seen of Epps on this side of the Ohio river the party went several miles over into Ohio and continued their search until late last night.

Epp, was arrested in Ironton by the police early Sunday night as he was attempting to board a freight train going to Columbus. The arrest was made by the Ironton Chief of Police. When arrested he denied his identity and swore that he had never been in Huntington, but as he fitted the description sent out from here, he was held and Chief Morris Davis notified of the arrest. Davis returned from Ironton with Epps this afternoon, and placed him in the county jail.

CHANCE FOR RECOVERY OF WILLIAM VINSON. Negro Who Did Stabbing Captured and Lodged In Jail After a Long Chase.
Huntington, W. Va., July 20.—[Special.]—William Vinson, of Catlettsburg, who was so seriously stabbed by Gus Epps, a negro, in this city, is yet alive and the physicians are hopeful of his recovery, notwithstanding his right lung was pierced several times by the keen-bladed knife. Vinson's friends are greatly enraged over the unwar-

ranted assault of the negro, and when the latter was brought here from Ironton, O., this afternoon, where he was captured, many threats were made and the negro was quickly hustled behind the bars of the Cabell county jail. Epps assaulted Vinson with a knife, thinking he was another man. Vinson, at the time, was en route from a hotel to the C. and O. passenger station. The negro was chased by a posse for five miles, finally swimming a stream and later crossing to Ohio in a leaky craft, where he was captured while boarding a freight train. He will be given a speedy trial.

gustave-epps-huntington-1903-07-19.A12:
Killed by Mistake.
William Vinson, a prominent young business man of Catlettsburg, Ky., was fatally stabbed in Huntington at 3 o'clock last Sunday morning by Gus Epps, a negro, who had mistaken Vinson for another man.

Epps, while passing the Huntington Hotel, was assaulted by three unknown white men, and half an hour later he passed Vinson, who was en-route to the passenger station, and, thinking he was one of his former assailants, he plunged a knife into his chest several times. Vinson's lungs were penetrated.

Epps tried to escape, but he was pursued by two policemen and several other persons who were in the hotel lobby. Epps was surrounded in a swamp west of the city, and 40 shots were exchanged by the negro and the posse. Finally the negro, after being injured, escaped in the darkness, and, running a mile farther, plunged into the Twelve Pole river to swim to the opposite shore. His pursuers were near, and a fusillade of bullets was turned toward him in midstream and he sank to a watery grave. Vinson was a relative of ex-Governor Bradley, of Kentucky.

henry-small-1903-07-21.A2:
The County of Chester-
field Stirred.

ARMED MEN ARE
SEEKING A NEGRO

Information Received is Very
Meagre.

ATTACK MADE ON
THREE WHITE WOMEN

Manchester Police Notified and on the Alert for the Criminal-The Names of the Victims Were Not Obtainable Last Night-A Telegram from Chester.
Excited men, armed with loaded shot-guns, and with thoughts of vengeance stirring their breasts, scoured Chesterfield county in the neighborhood of Centralla last night in a fruitless search after a flying negro fiend, who some hours earlier in the day committed, or attempted to commit, a criminal assault upon two, and possibly three, white women of the county. At the same time in Richmond and Manchester, toward which place the fugitive was supposed to be heading, a close watch was kept on the railway stations and other roads of ingress along which the man might come; but he came not, or had not come up to the early hours of the morning.

Scant in the extreme is the information obtained or obtainable concerning the affair, which is said to have caused great excitement in the county during the evening. Every available source was exhausted last night, and still nothing could be learned with any definiteness. Several had heard of the affair, and that there was an assault committed upon either two or three white women at or near Centralla by a negro man, who was afterwards chased by armed men, nobody seemed to doubt. But as for further details, there were none. Railway officials, police stations, car lines, private telephones and what not were utilized, but with equal effect. Sleeping men roused from their beds declared that they could throw no light upon the matter.

Manchester Notified.

Not even the hour in which the reported assault is supposed to have occurred could be ascertained. The first information came early in the evening in the shape of a notification and alarm to the Manchester police. Captain Lipscomb, just ready to go home to supper, was informed that an assault had been committed by a negro upon two ladies in Chester, and that the man was heading in the direction of Manchester, being chased by a mob. He drove at once to station No. 5, about a mile below Manchester, where he learned that the negro had turned in the direction of Petersburg, and there doubled on his track, and made for Richmond again. The manner in which he persisted in his course in this direction led Captain Lipscomb to believe that he was a Mnachester or Richmond man.

By this time, however, the negro had left the car tracks and was either hiding in the woods or working a short cut through the fields. It was impossible to block him. Captain Lipscomb returned to Manchester and set his officers on the watch, and a careful vigil was kept. Before he went, however, the chief told the men on the Petersburg car line, all of whom are armed, to arrest the negro and bring him here if they caught sight of him anywhere on the road.

Boarded Seaboard Train.

Communication was gotten through the Atlantic Coast Line operator with Chester and Drewery's Bluff, between which places the assault is said to have occurred, but neither the one nor the other could give any further details. Both had heard of the assault, but as for names, etc., they knew nothing. There was no night office open at Centralia. About midnight The Times-Dispatch correspondent at Chester, in response to a telegram, sent the following, which may be placed in the same category with the other accounts:

"News of assault not definite and unknown as to parties. Hear that three ladies were assaulted at Centralla this evening by a negro and the police of Manchester and Richmond were telegraphed to look out for him, as he had boarded a freight train on the Seaboard Air Line going north about 9 o'clock this evening."

The information as to the train was also given later to the Manchester and Richmond police, and the stations were watched, but without effect. It was too late to catch the freight, which came into Manchester about 10 o'clock, but Officer Wright at once posted himself at the depot, where he stayed until after midnight. The freight had just gone by when he got there. Up to the time that he left no signs of the fugitive appeared.

Conductors Knew Nothing.

As a last resort toward gathering some further facts in connection with the matter all the conductors and engineers of the Seaboard who had come in during the night were waked up, but they, like the others, could add nothing to the meagre information already in hand. They had seen nothing of the negro, nor had they heard of the assault.

According to the description received by the Manchester police, the negro who committed the crime is short, black and stout. He had on a brown suit of clothes and wore shoes which had no heels to them.
henry-small-1903-07-21.A5:
Account From Chester.
In the following special, received last night, the correspondent of The Times-Dispatch at Chester, gives a vivid account of the happenings of Tuesday:

Mrs. R. W. Thompson, living near "Bellwood's," in this county, a widow of sixty or more years, was attacked yesterday afternoon about 4:30 P. M. in her home and the same negro attacked and robbed Misses Thurston and Clement on their way home walking about one hour later, a short distance from Centralia Station.

Mrs. Thompson tells the following story of her awful experience. She says she had returned from a hospital in Richmond, where she had gone to be treated the same day about noon. That she laid down to rest in the afternoon while her tenant, Mr. Willie Sadler, had gone in the field to plow. About 4 P. M. she arose and went on the shady side of her house and sat in the door, which opened immediately on the yard without a porch and was reading a paper and enjoying the fresh air, when a burly negro of short, stout stature, between a black and mulatto, wearing an old black suit and black slouch hat, approached within a few feet of her before she was aware of him and asked that she give him something to eat. She replied that she had just arrived home, and that the man on the place had eaten all in the house at dinner and there was nothing to give him. He turned and started to go away, and, after getting some yards away, came back and asked for a drink of cool water, when she told him he could get fresh water from the well, which was about twenty feet from the door. His return and his peculiar forbidding countenance aroused her suspicion and this caused her to watch his movements closely.

He drew the water and drank from the bucket and she concluded that it would be better to show no fear by retiring to the house, so she sat in the door and eyed him. After he had drank, he returned by the door, and when about two steps away and opposite her, he sprang on her, seized her and bore her to the floor, telling her that if she made any noise he would kill her. She screamed with all her might, and he seized her with both hands on her throat and was choking her to insensibility, when she caught his underlip with one of her hands with all her might fighting him off.

This caused him to relax one hand from her throat, when she screamed again. Mr. Sadler, in the field, heard her screams and respondfied each time, and was unloosing his horse from the plow to come in, and
respondied each time, and was unloosing his horse from the plow to come in, and at her last scream he hallooed with all his might, "all right, I am coming." The brute evidently heard Sadler's last response, for he then released his grasp an dran off, without accomplishing his devilish designs.

Mrs. Thompson rushed from the house, not having herself heard Sadler, and started for the field, when Sadler came up, and on hearing the matter ran in the direction the fiend had gone, but not getting sight of him, he went to some neighbors, and they all began to hunt for the negro with guns.

The negro eluded them by fleeing through the woods near by, and evidently found his way to the electric road, near Centralia, and was going south from Mrs. Thompson's. When very near Centralia, a mile or more from his first crime, he met Miss Thurston and Miss Clement walking home from Centralia on the electric road. Miss Thurston had just had a five-dollar bill exchanged at Centralia for small change, and had the money in a satchel in her hand. The negro passed them and immediately turned and grabbed the satchel, tearing it out of the lady's hand, and the collision threw Miss Thurston to the ground, while the negro took to the woods. The young ladies screamed, and ran back to the station in a breathless condition, and, as soon as they could tell the story, a squad of citizens armed themselves and started in pursuit, and continued the search until night, without finding the fiend.

The negro described by the young ladies was identical with the one described by Mrs. Thompson, and was doubtless the same. The police authorities of Richmond, Manchester and Petersburg were notified, and Messrs. Myers and Sadler took the car for Petersburg at once, and walked the track back to Mrs. Thompson's, but did not see the man, and up to this morning nothing was known here if he has been caught. A rumor from Centralia this afternoon says he has been apprehended, but little reliance is attached to it.

The matter was reported to Sheriff W. C. Gill this morning at Centralia, who was on his way to Richmond. A prominent colored man at Chester told me today that he suspected that this fiend was the same man who entered Thompson's house a few years ago, and robbed it, and was caught and sent to the penitentiary for two or three years. He reasons that the negro having been released took this course for revenge. This is the first case of assault ever recorded in this vicinity, and the public sense has been aroused, and I was told at Centralia this morning that had the wretch been caught he would have been shot or swung up.

Well-Known Ladies.

All three of the ladies attacked are of highly respected Northern settlers.

Mrs. Thompson had a gun by her side
henry-small-1903-07-21.A7:
ATTACKED BY NEGRO.
THREE WOMEN ASSAULTED.
Assailant Eludes Pursuit in Chesterfield County.
Assailant Eludes Pursuit in Chesterfield County.

An unknown negro Tuesday assaulted three women in Chesterfield County within an hour, and though men armed with shotguns and other weapons, hunted for the negro for hours, bent upon wreaking dire vengeance upon him, he is still at large. The first was an attempt at criminal assault, and was made on a woman sixty years of age. The second assault was on two young girls, and the purpose in this instance was robbery.

While Mrs. R. W. Thompson was sitting on the porch of her home between Bellwood and Centralia Tuesday afternoon, a negro approached and asked for food. He was told that the servant was away and that he could get nothing. He then asked for water, and was pointed to the well.

After drinking, the negro started away, but suddenly came back and made a fiendish assault on Mrs. Thompson. Despite threats, Mrs. Thompson struggled desperately and screamed at the top of her voice. With almost superhuman strength she wrenched one hand from the negro's grasp, and seized him by the lower lip. While the desperate struggle was going on Mrs. Thompson never ceased her cries, and these, together with her brave struggles, saved her from the fiendish brute. A tenant on the place heard the cries, and came rapidly calling out as he ran. The negro fled. Mr. Sadler found Mrs. Thompson weak and helpless on the floor, trembling from the reaction of her brave struggle.

An hour later, as Miss Una Clement and Miss Bertha Thurston were walking to their home from Centralia along the track of the electric line, they came upon a negro setting on the track. It proved to be the same man who had attacked Mrs. Thompron. He arose and started to pass the two girls. As he got opposite he snatched a hand satchel from Miss Thurston. The girl brought her umbrell down over the negroe's head, and was rewarded by a blow that felled her to the ground, and her companion was thrown on top of her.

The negro then walked off, and Miss Thurston pursued him, a colored boy on a horse joining in the pursuit. Seeing that he was followed, the desperate negro drew a pistol, and pointing it at his pursuers, told them to go back.

The negro boy rode to Centralia as rapidly as his horse would take him, and gave the alarm. Soon every man in the community, well armed, was searching for the brute. News soon reached them of the first assault, and every nook and corner of the country was scoured. The negro was tracked to a swamp, and this was surrounded by pickets ready to shoot on sight. News was sent to Manchester and Richmond. Crews on the electric cars reported seeing a negro of the description going in the direction of Petersburg. Another had seen him going in the opposite direction. He apparently had doubled on his tracks and eluded his pursuers.

One negro was arrested Tuesday night with two ladies' pocketbooks on him, but Miss Thurston came to Manchester and declared he was not the one who assaulted her and her companion. The police are still on the watch.

Edward Pulliam and John Palthreo, the negroes arrested on suspicion of having committed the attacks on ladies in Chesterfield on Tuesday evening, had their cases continued in the Police Court until one of the ladies can come from Chesterfield to identify them. Both negroes claim to have come there direct from North Carolina.
henry-small-1903-07-21.A9:
CHASING NEGROES
Chesterfield Constables After a Gang of Them.
MINERAL MAN NOT THE ONE
Young Boy Kicked Yesterday by a Mule. Arrangements for the Coming Primary—Grand Jury Meets Again To-Morrow—Churches.
Manchester Bureau Times-Dispatch,

Vigorous efforts are being made by the constabulary of Chesterfield county to rout from the woods of a certain section of the place, beginning at Marx Addition and extending to Centralia or thereabout, a gang of negroes said to be responsible for sundry lawless acts recently reported, including the murderous attempt to rob the house of a citizen and the assault upon the three ladies on last Tuesday. Officers have been scattered throughout the neighborhood, and 'Squire Cheatham, who is directing the movements, said yesterday that he was determined to put a stop to the depredations of the outlaws. One of the constables stumbled across three of them in the woods the other night, and when they refused to halt fired several times at them, but so far as is known without effect. A young man out recently picking blackberries ran into a big negro sprawled full length on the grass—the personification of laziness. He seemed to have fixed himself there to stay. Over some sticks hanging over his head he had stretched some tin to keep the sun and the rain off, while he lay basking below.

As stated before, it is the determination of the officers to get rid of this gang, if they have to arrest every one. They believe that one of this number committed, or attempted to commit, the assault upon Mrs. Thompson Tuesday afternoon. Two negroes, supposed to be of the gang of tramps, were arrested Friday night by Officer Grant. They are Albert Baldwin and William Norwood. They are not thought, however, to have any connection with the assault.

NOT THE RIGHT ONE.

But scant success attends the efforts of the officers to locate the assailant of Mrs. Thompson, and it now appears likely that the criminal will never be apprehended. Charles McDonald, the man arrested at Mineral the other day, and who was generally believed to be the right one, turns out after all not to be the man. Mrs. Thompson and Miss Thurston came down from Centralia yesterday and took a look at him, but declared positively that he was not the proper person. Another negro was arrested at Emporia and was brought to the Manchester jail last night. The ladies will come down to identify him to-morrow.

THE PRIMARY ELECTION.

At a meeting of the chairmen of the Democratic Committees of Manchester, Chesterfield, and Powhatan, held July 23, 1903, it was ordered that a primary election be held in the city of Manchester and the counties of Chesterfield, Powhatan and Goochland, between the hours of 6 A. M. and 7 P. M. on Thursday, September 24, 1903, to nominate a candidate for the State Senate from the Sixteenth Senatorial District, and every candidate shall at least thirty (30) days prior to said election give notice in writing of his candidacy to the respective chairmen of the city and counties last above named.

And at the same time it was ordered that on the same day (September 24, 1903) and between the same hours, a primary election shall be held in the city of Manchester and in the counties of Chesterfield and Powhatan to nominate a candidate for the House of Delegates from said city and counties and at the same primary election in the county of Chesterfield to nominate a candidate for the House of Delegates from said county.

Candidates must give notice in writing at least thirty (30) days prior to said elections to the chairmen of the said city and counties, except candidates to represent Chesterfield alone, who shall only give notice to the chairman of the Chesterfield Committee.

Only qualified white Democratic voters shall vote at said elections.

henry-small-1903-07-21.A11:
CONSTABLE KILLS NEGRO.
The Latter Was Running Away to Evade Arrest.
Evade Arrest.
tch to The Evening Star.
ED. Ya. July 28

Evade Arrest.

Special Dispatch to The Evening Star.

RICHMOND, Va., July 28—Constable Moore of Chesterfield county shot and killed an unknown negro at Jarrett's, twenty miles below Petersburg, in Sussex county.

Moore had been sent to Jarrett's by Squire Cheatham to arrest a man who answered the description of the outlaw who assaulted Mrs. Thompson and Misses Thurston and Clement at Centralia last week. On his arrival at Jarrett's the officer saw the negro and started toward him to arrest him. As soon as the negro saw the constable he ran for the woods. The officer called three times for him to halt and then fired. The ball struck the negro in the left side and he died in a few minutes.

Nobody in the neighborhood can identify the dead man, but his description exactly answers that of the perpetrator of the outrage on Chesterfield ladies.
henry-small-1903-07-21.A12:
SHOT THE FLEEING NEGRO.
Posse of Constables Was After Him for Attacks on Women.
PETERSBURG, Va., July 27.—On Tuesday last an attempt was made by a negro to assault Mrs. G. W. Thompson at her home near Bellwood in Chesterfield county. The negro was driven off. The same evening the same negro attacked two young women near Centralia, a few miles out of Bellwood.

A negro answering his description was found by a posse composed of Constables Moore, Batte and Brown. As soon as he saw the constables he sprang through a window and ran away. Constable Batte fired three shots at him and he fell mortally wounded, dying shortly afterward. He gave his name as Henry Small, and said he was from Jacksonville, Fla., and that he had killed several men and was trying to keep clear of officers.
henry-small-1903-07-21.A13:
THE NEGRO
ASSAULTER
IS KILLED

One Wanted in Chester-
field Killed in Sussex.

FLED FOR WOODS ON
SIGHT OF OFFICERS
Bullet Brought Him Down and Ended His Life.

WAS IDENTIFIED BY
WOMAN HE ATTACKED

Body Scarred, Showing that He Had Been in Many Difficulties—Coroner's Jury Brought in a Verdict of Justifiable Homicide.
Troops on Duty at Boydton.
WAS IDENTIFIED BY WOMAN HE ATTACKED
(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

JARRATT, VA., July 27.—Henry Small, the negro who last week attempted a criminal assault on Mrs. Thompson in Chesterfield county, and later, the same day, assaulted Misses Clement and Thurston near Centralia, was shot and killed by officers of the law in Sussex county yesterday. He fled on the approach of the officers, and when a load of bird shot failed to stop him the officers opened fire with their pistols. One ball toook effect in his back, and the negro sprung into the air and dropped to the ground. He died in a few minutes.

Later Mrs. Thompson and one of the young ladies whom the negro robbed near Centralia arrived and identified the dead negro as the one who had attacked them. The coroner's jury viewed the remains and rendered a verdict of justifiable homicide.

On last Tuesday night Henry Small, a negro answering fully to the description of the man wanted for attempted assault on Mrs. D. W. Thompson, near Centralia, also for robbing two young ladies in the same neighborhood, got off the night freight train at Stony Creek, due there at a late hour of the night, and made his way to the farm of Mr. Luther Creath, and was taken into the home of Alfred Hill, a colored man, a tenant of Mr. Creath. He remained there until Sunday, and was employed for a day or more by Mr. Creath on the farm.

DESCRIPTION TALLLED.

He divulged to one of the Hill family that he had killed a man and was fleeing from justice. In some way Mr. Creath heard of this statement, and having read in his Saturday's mall of the affair at Centralia, noticed closely the description given and decided that this man measured up to the description in nearly every respect. His clothing, with the exception of the hat, tallled exactly.

He made known the whereabouts of this man and a posse was organized, consisting of W. H. Moore, constable; J. H. Batte and C. M. Brown

On Sunday evening these gentlemen, in a top buggy, drove down to Hill's, and, being partly concealed by the buggy, were close on the negro before he realized their purpose. He was on the outside of the house, but, before they could alight, sprang into the house and tried to escape by a rear door.

His pursuers took it for granted that he was well armed, and felt sure that he would give them serious trouble when he emerged from the house. In his excitement he either could not find the pistol it is claimed he possessed or some one had misplaced it.

BULLET TOOK EFFECT.

The officers tried to head him off, but he broke and ran. Only one barrel of Moore's gun being loaded with small shot, he fired at him and hit him in the hips and leg, his intention being to stop, but not kill him.

The negro continued to run, when the others fired at him three times with pistols. Only one ball took effect, but from this wound the negro soon died.

He claimed to be from Jacksonville, Fla., and said he had recently spent some time in and around Richmond. Se had several old scars upon him, having been shot and cut several times. There was a pistol wound in his temple, another in his wrist, and another scar extending clear across his abdomen, he having been badly cut at some time. A physician who was present at the inquest says he never saw more scars on a man so young. He looks to be about twenty years old, is dark, but not very black.

The officials of Chesterfled were notified of the occurrence, and were requested to have the ladies connected with the affair sent here in order that he might be identified. The morning train brought Mrs. Thompson and one of the young ladies who was robbed, and they feel sure he is the man.

His neck and wrists were scratched and the shirt first worn was badly torn. He had exchanged this for another while at Hill's. His lower lip was swollen and bruised. The verdict of the coroner's jury was that the killing was justifiable.
henry-small-1903-07-21.A17:
NEWS ITEMS.
Dr. Edward Hank, of Norfolk, son of Rev. J. D. Hank, was killed by the kick of a horse over the heart.

The cost of the Richmond strike so far, now nearly over, has been $200,000, of which the State pays $75,000.

The negro assailant of three ladies in Chesterfield was shot and killed by officers in Sussex county while fleeing. He was thoroughly identified.

Much to the regret of the people of this section Dr. J. S. Dill, of the Fredericksburg Baptist church, has accepted a call to Bowling Green, Kentucky.

Illinois is continuing to butcher the negro—not because he is a negro, but because of his fiendish inclination. Two more have been lynched, their bodies hacked to pieces and burned.

John E. Madden's $100,000 imported thoroughbred stallion "Mirthful," was burned to death in his stall at Hamburg Place, Kentucky, Monday. The barn was destroyed. The loss is about $200,000.

henry-thomas-parish-1903-03-08.A1:
A NEGRO FIEND IS LYNCHED IN FLORIDA
Tampa, Fla., March 9.— Henry Thomas, a negro, who attempted to criminally assault the 10-year-old daughter of Porter Keene, was lynched near Parish last night, after having admitted his guilt.
henry-thomas-parish-1903-03-08.A3:
BRUTAL NEGRO IS YYNGHED
Charged With Assaulting Small Girl.
DREW PISTOL ON THE MOTHER.
Said To Have Been Positively Identified by Victim—Was Taken In Charge by Posse of Citizens After Several Attempts.

Tampa, Fla., March 9.—Henry Thomas, a negro, who criminally assaulted the 10-year-old daughter of Porter Keene, was lynched near Parish last night after being positively identified by his victim and having admitted his guilty.

Thomas was captured yesterday afternoon 5 miles south of Parish and after being taken to the scene of his crime, was hanged to a tree.

The crime which Thomas committed was one of the most daring in this state, having taken place in broad daylight.

The 10-year-old daughter of Keene had been sent to the home of a neighbor to purchase some vegetables. The neighbor's home was only half a mile distant, and when the victim of the assault arrived there, she was sent a short distance from the farm to procure the vetables. There the negro saw her and immediately following, came up with and attempted to assault her, almost in sight of the farm house.

The little girl, when she finally managed to escape, ran towards her own home and the negro continued to follow her. Mrs. Keene, alarmed at her daughter's absence, had started in search of her, and immediately after she left her home, she saw her little daughter running toward her, with the negro in pursuit. Upon seeing Mrs. Keene, the negro drew a pistol on her and threatened to shoot if she came further in his direction. The alarm was immediately given, and posses of citizens began a search for the negro. He was located at several places, but managed to escape each time, until he was finally captured.
henry-thomas-parish-1903-03-08.A4:
NEGRO WAS LYNCHED FOR CRIMINAL ASSAULT.
Caught by a Posse of Citizens and Hanged to a Tree. Tampa, Fla. March 9—Henry Thom
Hanged to a Tree.

Tampa, Fla., March 9.—Henry Thomas, colored, who attempted to criminally assault the 10-year-old daughter of Porter Keene, Friday, was lynched near Parish last night after being positively identified by his victim and having admitted his guilt.

Thomas was captured yesterday afternoon south of Parish, and after being taken to the scene of his crime, was hanged to a tree.

Last Friday the 10-year-old daughter of Mr. Keene was sent to the home of a neighbor to purchase vegetables.

The neighbor's home was a half mile distant, and when she arrived there, the neighbor sent her to the garden to get the vegetables. There the negro saw her, and immediately followed, coming up with her and attempting the assault when only a short distance from the farm.

The little girl, when she finally managed to escape, ran toward home and the negro continued to run after her. Mrs. Keene, frightened at her daughter's long absence, went out to find her, and immediately after she left the house, she saw her little daughter running toward her, the negro following.

Mrs. Keene then proceeded to defend her daughter, but the negro drew a pistol on her and threatened to shoot her. Naturally, the helpless woman was badly frightened, but she returned to the house at once and secured a Winchester rifle, with which she returned to kill the negro, who ran, however, before she could get a shot at him.

The alarm was immediately given, and posses of citizens began a search for the negro. He was located at several places, but managed to escape each time.
henry-thomas-parish-1903-03-08.A12:
GOINGS ON IN FLORIDA.
Thos. S. Harris has been appointed postmaster at Live Oak.

Chipley has a new water works system and has granted a franchise for electric lights.

The Ocala Fair Association has been granted letters patent with $10,000 capital stock.

The Grand Lodge Knights of Pythias of Florida is holding its annual session in Jacksonville this week.

Sanderson is without either a school house or church. Both were demolished in the storm of ten days ago.

Secretry of the Navy Moody has accepted an invitation from Senator Mallory to visit Pensacola about the 25th inst.

William Audley, a negro, is in the jail at Tampa charged with splitting his wife's head open with an axe and then cutting it off.

LYNCHED FOR THE USUAL CRIME.
Fate of a Brutal Negro who Attacked a Little White Girl Near Parish, Florida.
Tampa, Fla., March 9.—Henry Thomas, colored, who attempted a criminal assault on the ten-year old daughter of Porter Keene, on Friday, was lynched near Parish last night, after being positively identified by his victim and having admitted his guilt.

Thomas was captured yesterday afternoon south of Parish, and after being taken to the scene of his crime was hanged to a tree.

Last Friday the ten year old daughter of Keene was sent to the home of a neighbor to purchase vegetables. The neighbor's was only a half a mile distant, and when the victim of the assault arrived there she was sent a short distance from the farm to procure the vegetables.

There the negro saw her and immediately following, came up and attempted to assault her almost within sight of the farm house. The little girl, when she finally managed to escape, ran towards her own home and the negro followed her. Mrs. Keene, alarmed at her daughter's absence, had started in search of her and immediately after she had left her home she saw her little daughter running toward her with the negro in pursuit. Upon seeing Mrs. Keene the negro drew a pistol on her and threatened to shoot her if she came further in his direction.

The alarm was immediately given and posses of citizens began a search for the negro. He was located at several places, but managed to escape each time until he was finally captured.

Magistrate's Small Fee.

While Judge Nero Pitchford was a Magistrate, many years ago, he was plowing about a half mile from home when one of his children came out and announced that a neighbor was at the house wanting to see him on important business. The weeds were about to outgrow the corn, but he climbed a large hill and was about worn out when he reached the house. The neighbor's wants were made known after much urging, two hours after the Judge arrived. After hearing the trouble elaborately explained, the Judge gave him some advice and started to return to his work.

The neighbor said: "Hold on. How much do I owe you?"

The Judge told him he did not make any charge, as the law would not allow it.

"Well," said the gentleman, after studying a few moments, "here's a nickel. I guess that will about pay you for your trouble."

The Judge told him he guessed it would, and went back to the distant bottom to take care of his horses, for it was then night.

THEIR OUTING OVER

District Guardsmen Break Camp Today.

WILL BE HERE TONIGHT

THE CAMP REGARDED AS GREAT SUCCESS.

Unpleasant Episode of Cutting Down a Tree in a Leesburg Cemetery.
WILL BE HERE TONIGHT
CAMP ORDWAY, LEESBURG, Va., August 1.—The annual encampment of the troops of the National Guard of the District of Columbia is a thing of the past. The brigade marched away from George's farm at 2 o'clock this afternoon and will be in Washington about 4 o'clock. Unless the weather should be too inclement, the troops will be reviewed on the White Lot by Col. John Biddle, Engineer Commissioner of the District of Columbia.

Because of their wet condition all tents were left standing, to be struck later, under the direction of the post quartermaster.

The last morning in camp was a dreary one owing to the fact that rain fell at intervals during the morning. Captain Parker, acting paymaster, paid those officers and men entitled to pay for the six months which ended the 30th of June.

To the strains of "The Star Spangled Banner," the flag was lowered before the brigade marched from the camp site. The band played appropriate airs as the column passed through Leesburg. Almost the entire population of the town was out to bid the soldier boys farewell.

The first section of the special train transporting the troops moved at 2:30 o'clock. The other two sections followed at intervals of ten minutes.

Regulars Start for Fort Myer.

Troops H and E, 2d United States Cavalry, started for Fort Myer at 11 o'clock this morning, the cavalrymen being cheered as they rode away by the guardsmen. The squadron will camp tonight at Dranesville and will reach Fort Myer about noon tomorrow.

The last night in camp was a quiet one, everybody being completely tired out, and all retired early. The surgeons report that nothing of serious nature from a medical standpoint developed as a result of the real service experienced by the guardsmen in the field during the maneuvers.

A spirited and carefully thought-out attack on Ft. Evans yesterday afternoon concluded the two days' maneuvers.

The attacking force was engaged from 4:30 o'clock in getting into position. The attack was a success. The result of the maneuvering Thursday was decidedly in favor of the defense, the latter locating and theoretically annihilating several or-
attack was a success. The result of the maneuvering Thursday was decidedly in favor of the defense, the latter locating and theoretically annihilating several organizations of the attacking force. The rumor that Colonel Urell had been taken prisoner proved to be without foundation, on the contrary Colonel Urell made several important captures. Without regard to who won, the maneuvers proved most valuable and instructive.

One of the Guardsmen Fined.

"CAMP ORDWAY, Leesburg, Va., August 1.—Received of Gen. Geo. H. Harris, commanding National Guard of District of Columbia, thirty-one dollars and eighty cents ($31.80) in full for fine imposed in mayor's court on James Poe of the 1st Separate Battalion.

"W. A. EDWARDS, Sergeant."

The foregoing document is the visible evidence of one of the most remarkable travesties in justice that ever occurred in a civilized country.

A year ago yesterday the citizens of Leesburg and its vicinity indulged themselves in the pleasantry of lynching a colored man named Craven, accused of murder, but who was never tried for the alleged offense. The lynching took place within the potter's field of Leesburg, the untried man being hanged from the limb of a tree therein.

The potter's field adjoins the southwestern limits of the camp and is apparently more neglected than is usual in the case of pauper cemeteries. Five or six days ago the sheriff of Loudoun county complained to General Harries that some party or parties unknown had started to cut down the tree. The sheriff furthermore said the general belief was that the attempt had been made by members of the 1st Separate Battalion.

As a result of the complaint and because public feeling was officially said to be running very high, the general directed Maj. Brooks to suspend passes within the 1st Separate Battalion and to keep his men out of Leesburg so far as practicable, believing that thus there would be complete avoidance of that friction which might easily be excited.

C. F. C.
james-poe-leesburg-1903-07-31.A4:
NEGRO GUARDSMAN CUT DOWN TREE AND FINED
Jas. Poe, Member of First Separate Battalion, Punished.
(Special to The Washington Times.)

LEESBURG, Va., Aug. 1.—Mayor White held a session of court at Camp Ordway on George's Farm here today and tried and convicted James Poe, a negro member of the First Separate Battalion of the National Guard of the District, on a charge of destroying county property. Poe was assessed $30 and costs for misdemeanor. The fine was paid.

Ever since the National Guardsmen established their camp on George's Farm, the tree on which Charles Craven, the alleged negro murderer was lynched, has been pointed out as one of the sights along the road.

The tree was located in the Leesburg paupers' field.

Craven was convicted of highway robbery several years ago, and a farmer, by name Wilson, served on the jury which found him guilty. After serving his term in the penitentiary, Craven met Wilson alone on the road near Herndon.

Wilson's body was found later in a gully by the road. This occurred the latter part of July, 1902. The citizens of Loudoun county formed a posse and ran Craven down on a farm contiguous to the camp grounds. He was accorded summary justice without trial.

The negro battalion of the Guard objected to the tree, and eight of the Guardsmen partially succeeded in chopping down the tree last Thursday. The authorities of the county apprised Gen. George Harries of the fact that the tree had been cut and warned him against permitting any of his men to further molest it.

On Friday morning the same eight negroes went down the road, armed with an ax, and felled the tree completely. As it fell, some of the members of the Second Cavalry, who were camped on the western side of George's farm, got a glimpse of the culprits, and gave pursuit. The negroes dashed up the road and abandoned their weapons. The cavalrymen called a halt, and opened fire on them with ball catridges.

The frightened negroes dashed through the cavalry camp, and passed General Harries' headquarters.

The cavalry men yelled across the field to halt them, and Sergeants Hartnett and Eberley, of Company E, Second Regiment, captured four men, and the guards of the day apprehended the remainder of the party. The eight men were incarcerated in the guard tents all day yesterday, and rumors were numerous.

The townspeople were indignant, and there was some talk of lynching the negroes after the town sergeant procured warrants for their arrest and brought them out of camp.

The prisoners were kept under a heavy guard, maintained until about noon yesterday, when Sheriff Russell and Mayor White, together with several deputies went over to General Harries and made a demand for the prisoners.

After considerable parley it was decided to hold trial in General Harries' tent. The eight negroes were arraigned on charges of cutting down a tree in a county cemetery. All pleaded not guilty.

After a trial which lasted for more than an hour Mayor White decided that the evidence against all but James Poe was inadequate and seven men were discharged. The maximum fine of $30 and costs was imposed on Poe. The costs were $1.80, which were paid together with the $30, by General Harries. The general, at the conclusion of the civil trial, ordered the men kept under guard and returned to their quarters. He will in all probability dishonorably discharge all of them from the Guard tomorrow.

of the District of Columbia are rapidly fading away. However, the one disagreeable incident of the recent outing near Leesburg, Va., will not soon be forgotten, it seems, by the local citizen soldiery. On four occasions Washington's brigade of organized militia has camped and maneuvered in the immediate vicinity of the Loudoun county town mentioned and never was there one word of complaint uttered until it became known, the latter part of last week, that a tree, from which a year before an untried man was lynched, had been felled. Several members of the District National Guard chanced to be nearby at the time the tree toppled over and they were taken into custody by a military guard. The prisoners were tried before the mayor of Leesburg, who accepted an invitation to hold court in Gen. Harries' tent. The verdict was that Private James Poe of the 1st Separate Battallion must pay a fine of $80, and, in addition, $1.80 as court costs. The fine and costs were promptly paid.

"The conviction of Private Poe was one of the most remarkable travesties on justice that ever occurred in a civilized country," declared an officer of the brigade of high rank who was present at the hearing. "There was not one word of evidence against him, it being clearly proved that the cutting had been done by a civilian—a colored man believed to be a resident of Leesburg. The atmosphere was laden with threats of lynching, and one citizen of Leesburg went so far as to announce, with unrestricted use of profanity, that he intended to 'git' Poe if he had to shoot the latter from a window.

"But evidence cut absolutely no figure at that amazing hearing last Saturday morning," added the officer. "A tree by the aid of which unpunished murder had been committed was evidently regarded sacred, especially by the law officers of Loudoun county and of Leesburg, and some one, guilty or innocent, had to be punished for the felling of it. Private Poe happened to be a colored man, and close by, and, therefore, he was considered a suitable person to be made the victim.

"The injustice that was perpetrated in this instance made a deep impression on Gen. Harries, and, as far as I have been able to learn, on the entire brigade. I am in a position to know that the National Guard of the District of Columbia, in consequence of the episode, will never again choose Leesburg or its vicinity as the site

After the breaking of camp last Saturday, as the brigade approached the town on its march to the railroad station, Gen. Harries sent instructions to the chief musician of the band to play straight military music and to eliminate such selections as 'Auld Lang Syne,' 'Carry Me Back to Old Virginia Shores,' and the like, the rendition of which is customary on such occasions. The imposition of the fine mentioned, it is clear, will result in the loss to Leesburg of the financial benefits that have accrued to the town heretofore by reason of the visits there of the local brigade."

Brigade Worked Hard.

One of the pleasant features of the recent outing was the presence of Colonel Rospopoff, military attache of the Russian embassy in this city. The verdict of officers and men is that Colonel Rospopoff is a cultured gentleman and a trained soldier. An old campaigner with the troops of the czar, by whom he is held in high regard, Colonel Rospopoff participated in the maneuvers of the District National Guard with zest. He underwent the "hardships" of the two days' of maneuvering, was drenched several times by the rain and slept on the wet ground without shelter. The visitor commended the brigade on the excellence of its work, and among other things, said:

"I had no idea that the National Guard worked so hard."

Cruise of Naval Battalion.

A board of survey, to consist of Lieutenant Sidney Bieber, paymaster; Lieutenant Joseph A. Dempf. 2d Division, and Lieutenant (junior grade) Lewis P. Clephane, 1st Division, all of the Naval Battalion, will assemble on board the Fern at 8 o'clock this evening to investigate an alleged shortage existing in the public property accountability of Sherburne G. Hopkins, late lieutenant commander, commanding the Naval Battalion, to determine the kinds and amount of property reported to be missing and to fix the responsibility therefor. This proceeding is by no means of an unusual nature.

Until all property matters are straightened out the annual cruise of the Naval Battalion, which, it had been announced, would begin the morning of the 16th and terminate the 27th, will not occur.

The battalion will perform small boat drill, signaling, pistol drill, infantry tactics, sword exercises, setting up exercises, navigation and drill with the guns carried by the U. S. S. Fern, with particular attention given to aiming drill and subcaliber practice, to be followed by actual target practice.

Pay for Camp Service.

Organization commanders will be kept busy during the next two weeks preparing pay rolls for the actual period of service of officers and enlisted men rendered during the ten days ended the 1st instant. The orders from headquarters directing the preparation of the rolls under the authority of section 14 of the act of Congress approved January 21, 1903, making provision for the payment of such of the organized militia of the District of Columbia as shall engage in actual field or camp service for instruction, were issued last Thursday and were published in full in The Star that day. The rolls must be prepared and forwarded to the adjutant general, D. C. Militia, not later than the 17th instant. The officials hope to be able to disburse the money by the 1st of September.
