Sent Back to Rules.
In the Circuit Court of Loudoun county yesterday in the case of B. V. White vs. Evening Star Publishing Company of Washington, a libel suit growing out of the publication of an account of the trial of one of the District of Colombia troops for cutting down a tree on which a colored man had been hanged by a lynching party, defendant claimed that process had not been so served as to give the court jurisdiction. The contention of the defendant was sustained and the case remanded to rules until plaintiff could find some one upon whom process could be legally served. The plaintiff was represented by Mr. John Alexander and the defendant company by Judge Norton, of this city, and Mr. E. E. Garrett, of Leesburg.
james-poe-leesburg-1903-07-31.A11:
Of Unpleasant Memory.

Last year's encampment at Leesburg was the most successful in the history of the local citizen-soldiery but it was marred by an unpleasant incident which occurred within the last twenty-four hours of camp.

About two years ago a negro named James Craven was lynched by citizens of Leesburg to a tree near the camp grounds for murdering a juror who helped to convict him. The tree was on the main road, and throughout the last encampment everyone who passed it remarked, "There's the tree on which that negro was lynched." This displeased the several hundred members of the First Separate Battalion, and while a sham battle was in progress, several members of the command sneaked over to the tree and with a few well directed blows of axes felled it to the ground.

Fired on Negroes.

Members of the Second Cavalry camped with the National Guardsmen saw the deed and opened fire on the negroes with loaded carbines. The negroes were finally captured and turned over to the civil authorities of Leesburg, and for fear they would not be accorded the best of treatment, General Harries had them tried in his tent at camp. The judge imposed a penalty of $30 fine on one of them who pleaded guilty. The fine was paid and the negro released. Later he was expelled from his company.

General Harries' action in surrendering one of his men to the authorities was severely criticised by officers of his staff and under him, and the way in which the Virginia authorities handled the case was also the subject of much unfavorable comment. This is assigned as the reason for the Guardsmen "never going to Leesburg again."

Found Ideal Site.

When the citizen-soldiers returned from Leesburg, Major Neumeyer, quartermaster, and commissary general, went to Harpers Ferry and returned several days later with the news that there was an ideal camp site near that famous old place, and General Harries said at that time that it was not unlikely the 1904 encampment would be held in that vicinity. It was also said that a joint camp of regular soldiers and the militia of the District of Columbia and Maryland would be held a great distance from Washington, but this will in all likelihood be abandoned.

The site selected by General Corbin cannot be had until September 25, which is regarded as too late for National Guardsmen to participate in an outing of ten days. Most of the Guardsmen are employed by private corporations and storekeepers, whose business begins to get heavier in September and October, and consequently they could not spare their employees for ten days.

Longer Outing Probable.

At the conclusion of last year's outing, General Harries said he thought the boys liked the camp, and would stand for two weeks or fifteen days. It is highly probable that the coming encampment will be four or five days longer than any previous one. General Harries talked over the project with officers of the Guard, and the regular army who were in camp while it was running at its smoothest, and they all agreed that a fifteen-day encampment would afford more opportunities for the District boys to become thoroughly acquainted with soldiering during times of strife, and he placed himself on record as saying that he would make this year's outing four or five days longer than the others.

The regular army pay allowed the boys while in camp will be given them this year also. The pay of the troops for the six months' service, ending July 1, will be distributed by Capt. Andrew Farker on the last day in camp this year, and the regular army pay will be handed to the men after they return. It is the purpose of those in command to make everything as agreeable and inviting as possible, in order to get the highest possible number of men in camp.

A Busy Spring.

This winter has been, and the spring will continue to be, a busy one for the Guardsmen. In addition to their regular rifle practice and drills, they have had a rigid inspection, and another one is slated for next week. The last inspection was a preliminary one by Adjt. Gen. Lloyd M. Brett, preparatory to the inspection by a regular army officer in April. The War Department officials have designated Capt. Lloyd M. Brett, U. S. A., to make the second inspection. General orders No. 3, relative to the inspection, were issued from headquarters yesterday. The order follows.

"Capt. Lloyd M. Nacogdoches, La., Special.—This town has a population of 5 000 inhabitants of which one-fourth are colored and one-fourth own their homes. Steward died from lick on the back of his head. This is a very unpleasant place to live at some seasons of the year. In a community 12 miles from this place
there have been three preachers whipped and not less than 12 or 15 other men beat up. Rev. Steward died from lick on the back of his head. NEGRO TAKEN FROM HIS HOME.
Mob Believed to Have Killed Jim Pleasant, a Prosperous Black.
Mob Believed to Have Killed Jim Pleasant, a Prosperous Black.

Nacogdoches, Texas, January 30.—The sheriff and city marshal received a telephone message this afternoon from Appleby stating that a crowd of masked men visited Jim Pleasant's house on the night of the 28th instant, five miles east of the village, and shot the door to his dwelling full of holes and fusilladed the building generally with six-shooters and shotguns. Pleasant was carried off by the mob and it is supposed that he was killed, as he has not been seen or heard from since the night of the shooting. Pleasant was a prosperous negro and lived in the middle of a negro colony in that section of the county. The report to the officers is to the effect that the entire negro colony are terror stricken and are leaving their homes in droves. The sheriff, with a posse, has gone to the scene of the trouble, and will make a thorough investigation. Trouble has been brewing between some of the negroes and a few of the whites for some time and
jess-robertson-libby-1903-01-28.A4: it is the opinion of the officers that the attack on Pleasant will terminate the trouble.
jess-robertson-libby-1903-01-28.A5:
KUKLUX AT WORK.
Said to Have Terrorized the Negroes in Naeogdoches County. Nacogdoches, Tex., Jan. 31.—Constable Watson and Deputy Morris went to Liberty, in the eastern part of this county, where the negro population are being terrorized by what is regarded by some as an organized band of Kuklux. Negroes have been forced to

leave their homes since Christmas. Jess Robertson was taken from home and his horse whipped to death a few nights ago, and Wednesday night the band went to the home of Jim Morris, a negro schoolteacher, fired into the house, ran his family from home and carried him away. Morris has not been found yet, and the supposition is that he was murdered and his body burned in his barn. His clothes were found in the woods some distance from the house. Great excitement prevails.

Nacogdoches, Tex., Feb. 3.—Eight nogroes in the Libby community have been whipped and forced to leave.
jess-robertson-libby-1903-01-28.A9:
Kill Blacks and Destroy their Homes
REIGN OF TERROR AMONG THE NEGROES IN NACOG. DOCHES CO, TEXAS, BECAUSE OF WHITECAPS. Men Murdered and Women Spirited Awuy.

NACOGDOChes, Tex, Feb. 7. Because of a seeies of outrages perpetrated by whitecaps, intense excitement prevails among the Negroes in the extreme and isolated portion of Nacogdoches county, where a large colony of them has lived for years.

These Negroes besides buying and paying for their homes. have also built substantial churches and schoolhouses. Now this colony is likely to be depopulated, as the terror stricken colored people are fleeing in every direction.

Last Wednesday night a band of masked men went to the residence of Jim Pleasant, colored, and fired several shots into the door. Pleasant and his wife ran out the back door and he was captured and carried to the woods. His wife and babe escaped. Pleasant's clothes were found the next day, but no trace of him of a been found, although Constable Watson, Deputies Morris and Slay and several citizens have looked two days and nights.

As the whitecappers returned and burned Pleasant's barn. It believed that he was murdered and his body burned.

Last week the same band went to the home of Jesse Robertson, colored, ran his family from home and beat him into insensibility. Robertson swore out warrants again verbal parties whom he claims to have zd, but he has since disappeared and no trace of him can be fonud.

The following note was found this morning tacked to the door of another colored citizen near Libby:

"Jim Anderson: You are notified to leave here in four days or we will kill you. WHITECAPPERS."

Anderson is a quiet and well-to do negro and has never been known to get into any kind of trouble.

The county officials are making every effort to capture the ring leader whose name is known. He is in hiding in the dense pine woods near Libby. It is alleged by the officers here that whitecappers put Jim Pleasant away in order to obtain possession of Pleasant's wife.

A number of excellent recipes are presented in the March Delineator. The younger members of the household, gifted with a sweet tooth, will probably find pleasure in trying the several kinds of meringues, a confection seldom attempted in the home, though it appears from the recipes comparatively simple. The more practical-minded housewife will find some useful suggestions in an article on the uses of the bean, and also in the paper on ragouts. The pages of illustrated cookery, showing a St. Patrick's luncheon, constitute a pleasing display.

Houston, Tex.—The reign of terror among our people in Nacogdoches county continues. A small settlement ten miles from Nacogdoches is the latest scene of whitecap outrages. Ten were tied to trees and beaten unmercifully and others were warned to leave. Jim Anderson was shot to death in the woods, where he took refuge. Many others are missing. A dozen homes have been burned. Afro-Americans are fleeing to Oklahoma by the score.

jim-scott-lonoke-1903-06-08.A2:
KUKLUXING IN LONOKE
Good Citizens Are Determined to Put a Stop to It.
Kukluxing in Lonoke county has become so common that it has aroused the indignation of the better element of the people, and they have started a movement to put a stop to it and prevent further stigma upon the county by such disgraceful conduct on the part of a few. A telegram from Lonoke to the Little Rock Gazette of Sunday says:

J. A. Wilcox was arrested this morning at 10 o'clock on Front street charged with being one of the white-cappers who shot into the negro camp, five miles from here, Monday night. Wilcox is a farmer and lives in the vicinity in which the shooting took place. He is the third man to be arrested on the charge, and Sheriff Walls thinks there will be other developments next week.

W. P. Trimble and Bill Counts, two farmers, who were lodged in jail last night, seem to know nothing of the shooting. A Gazette representative called at the jail this morning and was escorted upstairs by Sheriff Walls. Count had little to say, but he did say that he was not guilty and heard the shooting nearly a mile away last Monday night, after 10 o'clock.

Trimble said he was surprised when the officers arrested him on this charge, as he was in bed asleep near where the shooting occurred, and was aroused by the reports of the guns, which lasted for several minutes. He did not see any one pass his house.

When questioned as to whether he knew the negroes were camped near his house he said he had understood there were three negroes from town out there.

The arresting of Wilcox, Counts and Trimble is causing much sensational talk in the neighborhood in which they live. The whitecapping practice has been going on near there for some years. The band of whitecappers refuses to allow a negro to work or live in that vicinity, or in the adjacent neighborhoods. This band is supposed to be the one that took the life of Bob Anderson, a harmless old darkey, who had lived here with his family for twenty years.
jim-scott-lonoke-1903-06-08.A3:
Anderson's shoes were found at the end of a foot-log a mile away, as if he had pulled them off and gone into the creek or tried to cross the stream. It is thought the whitecappers put his shoes there. Morris East and Jim Scott, the other two negroes who were shot at, were in town today, and detailed the facts to the writer, and said Anderson had off his shoes when the shooting took place, as he was preparing to go to bed. Scott says the whitecappers shot four times at him, and East says they shot a number of times at him.

Both are young negroes, twenty-five or twenty-six years old, and say they never have been into any trouble.

All the whitecappers had shotguns, and masks over their faces, the negroes say. Both negroes said John Weaver gave them permission to cut the timber at the place at which the shooting took place.

When the news of the outrage reached Lenoke Judge George W. Chapline Hon. Joe T. Robinson, Sheriff A. J. Wallis and his deputies, with at least fifty other good citizens, went to the scene of the tragedy and are still diligently pushing the search for prisoners and state's evidence.

Hon. Joe T. Robinson, one of the leading attorneys in the state, will push the prosecution, notwithstanding the prisoners wanted to retain him to defend them.

Many negroes have left their crops in the vicinity in which the shooting occurred. The affair is very much regretted by the good, law-abiding citizens of Lonoke, who will be a unit in making up money and assisting in the prosecution of the guilty parties. Judge Chapline thinks it is only a matter of time until whitecapping will be stopped.

The examining trial of the three men arrested will probably take place next Tuesday.

The citizens of Lonoke are determined that the good name of the town shall not suffer from such affairs, as several which have taken place, as this one did, some distance from Lonoke, have been charged up to Lonoke.

john-dixon-sparta-1903-08-03.A1:
LYNCH LAW FEVER.
Delaware is on the eve of another lynching if 300 men armed with shotguns and pistols who are in three separate posses succeed in catching Fletcher Hollis, a desperate negro of Smyrna aged 22 years, who last night shot and fatally wounded Constable James D. Wright at Clayton, one mile from Smyrna, while resisting arrest. The bullet struck Wright just below the heart, but by first hitting a button its course was deflected. The doctors believe it went downward and lodged in the pit of his stomach. Drs. Harmonson and Grier, who attended the victim, say they fear an internal hemorrhage, in which event death will speedily ensue. The town was so excited over the tragedy that the negro managed to escape after holding several pursuers at bay with his smoking pistol. As he is well known his capture is looked for hourly. Constable Jones and Constable Wright, of Clayton, were cooperating in an effort to arrest Hollis on the double charge of shooting at a man in Dover last Saturday night and creating a disturbance at the Friendship colored camp-meeting, four miles from Smyrna, Sunday evening. Neither constable was armed. When they saw the negro in front of the Hotel Stockle in Clayton at 7 o'clock yesterday evening Wright approached and said to him: "I want you." "No, you don't want me," was the reply. "Oh, yes, I do and I will take you," Wright rejoined. At this juncture the negro quickly drew a big pistol and, aiming it at Wright's head, shouted: "You won't take me!" Wright, who up to this time had not been assisted by Constable Jones, because of the latter's failure to have a pistol, suddenly seized the negro and wheeled him around. He hoped that by doing so he would have the pistol pointed away from him. Before he could accomplish this Hollis pulled the trigger and the bullet entered Wright's body. Wright, who is 50 years old, did not fall, but succeeded in walking to the hotel steps, where he collapsed and was carried into the hotel and physicians summoned. Constable Jones started in pursuit of the fleeing murderer after a bystander had gotten a pistol for him. As soon as he had fired the negro ran down the road toward Smyrna, pointing his smoking weapon backward as he ran and warning the pursuers. He soon entered a nearby cornfield and started across the country.

Heavily manacled and in the custody of Sheriff M. M. Berry, of Hancock county, Georgia, John Dixon, a negro charged with having feloniously assaulted Mrs. McLeon, a prominent white lady of Sparta, arrived in Macon at noon yesterday after barely escaping death at the hands of an infuriated mob. On Sunday night Mrs. McLeon had occasion to enter the backyard to quiet a vicious dog and was just returning to the house when she was set upon by the negro. She screamed lustily for help, and made heroic efforts to defend herself. A woman neighbor, hearing the cities for help, rushed to the assistance of the struggling woman, and after fighting the frantic woman for a short time the negro fled. Word was sent immediately to Mr. McLeon, who was attending to some business in Sparta, and he started on a hunt for his wife's assailant. Yesterday morning, with Sheriff Berry, McLeon found Dixon and made desperate efforts to shoot him, but was prevented. A mob quickly gathered to deal out swift justice to Mrs. McLeon's assailant. It was a race to the depot be ween Sheriff Berry and the mob, and the Hancock county officer won by a small margin. He had just placed his prisoner on the train when the leaders of the mob appeared at the depot, but before any action could be taken the conductor gave orders for the engineer to go ahead.

George Hearshey, 19 years old, while hunting squirrels on his father's farm near Hartford City, Ind., yesterday, was approached by two prowling negroes. They seized the boy, searched his clothing for money and, finding none, tore his clothing from him and mutilated him with a knife. The boy succeeded in reaching his home. He told his story, and his father gave the alarm, mounted a horse and called for volunteers to wreak vengeance on the negroes. Two hundred men and boys joined in the chase. Neighboring farms and towns were warned by telephone and the country was scoured. No trace of the negroes was found. The hunt proceeded until nightfall. Sheriff Morigal, with a detachment of deputies and police, followed the mob to prevent a lynching, if possible.

SAVED BY HER CRIES.
Negro Attempted to Assault Young Woman Near Sparta.
Macon Ga. Aug. 3.—John Dixon, a
Woman Near Sparta.

Macon, Ga., Aug. 3.—John Dixon, a negro 20 years of age, was brought to the Macon jail this afternoon charged with assault upon the daughter of a farmer near Sparta, in Hancock county. Her screams caused the negro to desist. He was subsequently captured and taken to the jail in Sparta, but as mob was forming, the sheriff spirited Dixon to the train and lodged him here for safe keeping.

The young woman was uninjured.
john-dixon-sparta-1903-08-03.A3:
TRIED TO KILL PRISONER.
Sheriff Saves Negro from Man Whose Wife He Assaulted.
[BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.] on. Ga., Aug. 3.—After a close ra

Macon, Ga., Aug. 3.—After a close race with a furious mob, Sheriff Berry of Hancock County reached here this afternoon with John Dixon, a negro, seventeen years old, who last night assaulted Mrs. Henry McLean, wife of one of the best known planters of that county.

Mrs. McLean was alone at her home, and went into the back yard to quiet a dog. As she was returning to the house the negro set upon her, but was frightened away by her cries. When the negro fled Mrs. McLean fainted, and was still unconscious when her husband returned.

When he learned the facts, with a party of neighbors he started in pursuit of Dixon, who had been captured by the Sheriff. McLean tried to shoot the negro while in the Sheriff's hands, but was prevented by the officer. The posse then went for reinforcements and the Sheriff made for Sparta, where he caught a train to this city leaving Sparta just as the leaders of the mob rode up.

john-farrow-maysville-1903-06-16.A3:
TAKEN TO COVINGTON.
Lynching Prevented by Prompt Action of Maysville Officers.

Maysville, Ky., Feb. 3.—[Special.]—Charley Saunders, Tom Manns and Ed Morrison, all colored, charged with assaulting John Bruer Farrow, were hurried off to the Covington jail this afternoon to avoid a mob that was coming to-night from Mt. Carmel, Mt. Gilead and Orangeburg. Several hundred excited men followed the prisoners from the jail to the depot, and officers kept the crowd back with pistols. Men from Farrow's neighborhood have been quietly watching the jail, and there was no concealment that a mob was coming. The transfer to Covington was unexpected, else the movement would have been thwarted. The demonstrations toward the prisoners at the depot made them tremble. Charles G. Calvert, a prominent farmer of Orangeburg, was so frantic in his efforts to stop their removal that he was arrested.

Charley Saunders made full confession before the grand jury to-day, putting most of the blame on his two companions. Indictments were returned against all three prisoners for burglary and for shooting with intent to kill.

Farrow's physicians have hope of his ultimate recovery.

THEY ARE HERE! And They Will Aid the Civil Authorities in Preserving Peace.
In accordance with a request of Judge James P. Harbeson of the Circuit Court, and in obedience to orders from GovernorBeckham, Adjutant General David R. Murray yesterday dispatched a body of soldiers to this city to be present during the trial of the three Negroes charged with assault on Mr. J. B. Farrow at his home near Mt. Gilead some months since.

The first contingent arrived over the L. and N. last evening and the men are quartered at the Courthouse.

The second quota came at 10 o'clock this morning from Louisville by way of Covington. accompanying Sheriff J. R. Roberson in charge of the three prisoners.

General Murray, who by the way is a veteran of the Civil War and knows what real fighting is, is in chief command, while Major Nelson J. Edwards of Covington is in immediate command of the troops, whose officers are Captains Morris Robinson and Hal Griffith of Louisville, Captain Gordon of Frankfort, Captain Peake of Covington, Lieutenants Blakley and Bert Fuhrmann of Covington and Lieutenant Lindenberger of Louisville.

Accompanying the Frankfort contingent was a Gatling gun, while the Louisville delegation brought a Hotchkiss, which, with the smaller arms, are sufficient to suppress any mob that may confront them.

THE LEDGER regrets exceedingly that any occasion should have arisen for the presence in our midst of this warlike demonstration, but the demoralized element of the city and county is alone responsible.

It should be borne in mind that these troops are not here simply to protect three worthless Negroes.

They are here to preserve the peace and to protect the lives and property of the citizens; they are here at the request of the Circuit Judge of this District; they are here by command of the Governor of the Commonwealth; they are here to prevent a repetition of the scene of some three years ago; they are not here to take the initiative in any demonstration. They are subject solely and alone to the orders of Judge Harbeson and of Sheriff Roberson, whom the people of this county have chosen as their chief peace officers.

It is the duty of every good citizen to stand by the law and to see that there is no occasion for the use of any force on the part of the state's power to preserve the peace.

THE LEDGER begs that our citizens will see to it that there is no attempt at violence.

Trial in Kentucky Was Con ducted Under Protection of Soldiery.

SWILLE, KY. June 18—70

MAYSVILLE, KY., June 18.—The trial of the three negroes, Sanders, Mann and Morris, continued under protection of soldiers to-day.

Sanders confessed complicity in the murderous assault on the Farrow family and was sentenced to five years in prison. He testified that Mann and Morris were the direct perpetrators of the assault.

In the afternoon Mann and Morris also were convicted of shooting with intent to kill, and each was sentenced to five years in the penitentiary. The three negroes will be tried for burglary to-morrow, as that crime was committed at the time of the murderous assaulting of the Farrow family, and it is expected that each will be given an additional sentence of ten years. J. B. Farrow is not expected to live and the Commonwealth's attorney has reserved the right in event of the death of Farrow to have the three negroes pardoned and then tried for murder, so that they can be executed. It is thought the burglary cases can be disposed of to-morrow so that the troops will accompany the prisoners to the penitentiary at Frankfort.

Immediately on reassembling of Court yesterday morning the Commonwealth rested, and the Attorneys for defense put Sanders on the stand, who, in chief and on cross-examination, told substantially the story printed yesterday, emphasizing the statement that Manns was the leading spirit in the airfair and dragged him into it.

Charles Sanders, colored—Live in Maysville; know Tom Manns and Ed. Morris; Manns and I have been together frequently; Manns and Morris were with me at Farrow's house Sunday night, February 1st;—and then witness practically repeated the statements made on his own trial.

EAGLES HOLD A CONVENTION

Fifth Annual Meeting of the Order Convenes in Tammany Hall,
New York.

NEW YORK, Sept. 1.—The fifth annual convention of the Fraternal Order of Eagles began today at Tammany hall and will continue during this week.

This order originated in Seattle six years ago and is strongest in the west and northwest. It is expected that 10,000 of the 150,000 members in the United States and Canada will be here before the day is over.

Special trains from British Columbia, Boston, Baltimore and St. Louis brought delegations from the Pacific slope, New England and the south and southwest.

The New York aerie has made extensive arrangements for the entertainment of the visitors and Tammany hall is elaborately decorated. After calling the morning session to order an adjournment was taken until afternoon.

The committee on credentials has not yet finished its work. Mayor Low will review the parade of the Eagles tomorrow at the Worth monument.

ST. JOSEPH, Mo., Sept. 1—The R. T. Davis Mill and Manufacturing company of St. Joseph, with a branch house in Kansas City, was declared bankrupt today and Charles F. Enright was appointed receiver by B. J. Woodson, referee in bankruptcy. This is the pioneer miling firm of north-west Missouri and manufacturer of the "Aunt Jemima" brand of goods. Liabilities are said to be about $350,000 with assets, including plant, $500,000. The heaviest creditors are local banks and capitalists.

Many Reported Leaving Shawneetown, Ill., in Haste.

NO TROUBLE THERE YET
Passengers on the Evansville packet today report more or less suppressed excitement at Shawneetown, Ill., above Paducah on the Ohio river. A race riot is feared by many, and the negroes are reported to be leaving on every boat, and some are leaving afoot.

Shawneetown, it is stated, recently inherited a large crowd of stray negroes, from the exodus following the Danville, Ill., and Evansville, Ind., race riots and the people have been wanting to get rid of some of them for quite a while.

Night before last a mob of 50 men went to the jail and demanded John Griffin, colored, of Jailer Galloway. Griffin is charged with attempting to criminally assault Mrs. Joseph Hobbs, a white woman, who saved herself from harm by screaming. Griffin was arrested a short time afterwards.

Jailer Galloway met the mob leaders and reasoned with them, and finally, seeing that it did no good, he armed himself and defied them. He spoke to the men from the jail door and told them that anyone attempting to force the jail door would do so at his peril.

The mob made several attempts to batter down the door, despite the threats of the jailer, but could not accomplish anything. About daylight it dispersed.

The incident has produced considerable feeling, many of the negroes inciting hot-headed white people by openly siding with the negro in jail. While cooler heads may prevent trouble, a lot of the colored population is emigrating to be on the safe side.

NEWS OF THE WEEK EDITORIAL NOTE AND COMMENT.
The expectation that there would be "something doing" in the postal fraud cases this week proves well founded. There are seven more indictments, and, besides, Beavers is under arrest at last.

The president's announcement concerning his future policy in appointing men to the more important positions in the consular service deserves even more praise than it has elicited. He will select only those men who have already demonstrated their fitness in subordinate positions. This is a policy of progress and of practical civil-service reform. May there be no backward step.

It is not alone the highly disturbed and unsatisfactory condition of the labor market which is leading large railroad and other corporations to postpone contemplated improvements, as reported in a Pittsburg dispatch. Quite as important as an inducing cause is the condition of the securities market and the scarcity of available capital. This is the real determining factor in the matter.

"Sam" Parks, convicted of extortion and only out of Sing Sing pending appeal proceedings, led the labor parade at New York Monday. This is not the way for labor unions to win the support of the public. Even if the man has been wrongfully convicted, it would be more becoming for him to take a less conspicuous place until his innocence is established beyond a doubt. Significant it is that during the march yesterday hisses as well as cheers greeted his appearance.

The example of the sheriff at Danville, Ill., who stood his ground and defended the jail successfully against a mob of lynchers, is having its certain salutary effect all over the state. It was seen last week in Shawneetown, when a "niggerhunting" mob assailed the jail there, only to be met by Jailer Galloway in so determined a manner that it slunk off without making the promised assault. So it will usually be where the guardians of public order display a knowledge of their duty and an unmistakable determination to do it.

Twelve of 14 indicted citizens of Danville, Ill.,—the mayor of the place has referred to them as "highly respectable" have been found guilty of participation in the lynching riot there some weeks ago, and given an indeterminate sentence to prison. One of them is a woman. This is a wholly exceptional case of rigorous application of law to lynchers, and it cannot but have exceptionally salutary effect. It will take the heart right out of the lynching business in that place at least, and its influence will be felt in the country beyond. It is the only effective way of dealing with the lynching evil.

The situation at Beirut, according to Admiral Cotton, is evidently improving, and with Nazim Pasha, the vali or governor of Syria, on the scene, there is now little to fear. The American admiral, since he arrived at the port, appears to have acted with poise and discretion. If the coming of the squadron had a belligerent effect upon the Christians and Moslems of the town, the admiral himself was not responsible. He deserves praise for his refusal to heed the appeal from some of the inhabitants that he land marines, since it was not his business, as he is said to have replied, to interfere in a quarrel between Ottoman subjects. An admiral who can return such an answer, under those conditions, evidently has a cool and level head.

There was no written agreement to divide the patronage in Delaware, says Senator Ball of that state. "After the 'election Senator Allee and I were in 'Washington and officials of the administration forced us to come to an agreement about the apportionment of the federal appointments.' It was a verbal agreement. This account differs from that of Senator Allee, who said that the contract was drawn up, signed, sealed and deposited with the government. The two senators, however, agree that there was an agreement. That it was in reality verbal is probable. Boss Tweed once gave this advice, "Don't write; send word," and it was based on the principle that a thing in writing may return to plague a man. It is surprising if the politicians mixed up in Delaware patronage have ignored Tweed's fundamental rule of conduct.

Gov Jelks's reference to peonage in his recent annual message to the Alabama Legislature was, on the whole, very satisfactory treatment of the question, although some southern newspapers affirm that he did not express his views with sufficient promptness for the good of the state. Gov Jelks condemns peonage unreservedly, and lectures the state courts because the cases lately prosecuted were exposed, not through their instrumentality, but through the federal court. So sound an expression of opinion can be accepted, doubtless, as that of all the sober-minded, intelligent people of Alabama. In railing at northern newspapers because of the "sensation" they made out of the peonage cases, the governor cheapens his message somewhat. Abuses everywhere invariably entertain a grudge against the press that casts publicity upon them.

An amendment to the Grand Trunk Pacific railroad bill providing for full government ownership of the proposed transcontinental line received 50 votes, as against 135 in the Canadian House of Commons. The idea of government ownership of railroads is much stronger in Canada than in the United States. The Intercolonial is already a government property. The conservative party, through its leader, recently proposed a substitute for the Laurier Grand Trunk bill, which would involve government ownership and operation of certain lines. And under the Laurier bill itself, now passed by the House of Commons, a half of the new transcontinental line is to be built by the

---

government and then leased simply for 50 years. In the United States no such conditions yet exist. Railroad monopoly is substantially a private monopoly here.

The New Jersey court has made short work of the criminal charges of manslaughter against President Cassatt of the Pennsylvania railroad and other high railroad officials. The judges hold—and the three are unanimous—that no measure of personal responsibility attaches to the eminent defendants. The chief reason for this decision evidently is that no sand was placed on the slippery rails along which the trollly car slid to destruction. Inasmuch as there was no sand used, it follows that the employe, or employes, who failed to obey the rules in that particular are responsible for the tragedy, while the high officials are innocent of any criminal negligence. Evidently, in the opinion of the court, it is now the duty of the grand jury to find the men whose duty it was to sand the rails and "sock it to them." Nine children, it is certain, lost their lives in that trollly accident in an inexcusable manner.

Mr Chamberlain must see things to encourage him, but to an outsider nearly everything that happens emphasizes the opposition he must encounter in saving the empire by preferential tariffs. A few weeks ago 14 English and Scotch professors of political economy, connected with the leading universities, issued a manifesto against his tariff schemes. Probably Mr Chamberlain would not mind opposition of that character; professors may not count, even in Britain. But the powerful colonial secretary must realize the seriousness of the almost unanimous condemnation of his proposals by the British trades union congress. That organization has some slight claim to speak for the wage-earners of the kingdom, and the vote at least indicates that the working class, without whose support Mr Chamberlain's cause is hopeless, sadly need education in the advantages that a dear loaf will bring to them.

The government report on the cotton crop is decidedly damaging for the corner. There has been continued improvement in condition, and, while late and still exposed to climatic dangers, the crop at present is much above the average in promise. Expends Another $5,000,000 In Building New Vessels With More Tonnage Contracted For. New York, Jan. 10.—The International Mercantile Marine Company has issued a call for another 10 per cent, or $5,000,-000 of the $50,000,000 for which the underwriting syndicate holds itself liable. This money will be applied for payment of extra tonnage on new ships, four of which are now being built. In addition about as many ships are now under
construction at British ship yards. The vessels now under way will range from 10,000 to 15,000 tons, and while designed chiefly for freight will also have ample accommodations for saloon passengers as well as steerage passengers. Most if not all the new ships will carry the flag of the Atlantic Transportation Line, which is one of the constituent companies of the combine.

ODELL WANTS PLATT
ELECTED SENATOR.

Gives Out Emphatic Interview Calling On Supporters To Vote For the Easy Boss.

New York, Jan. 10.—In reply to questions as to his attitude toward the re-election of Senator T. C. Platt, Gov. Odell to-day made the following statement:

"I am for Senator Platt's re-election to the Senate unequivocally and unreservedly, and I believe that the Republican party offers him this renewed honor because of his service to it, and any rumors which may have been in circulation to the contrary are false and unreliable. I shall not only ask but expect my friends to aid in this direction and I shall do all in my power to accomplish this result."

The statement was made by the Governor subsequently to a conference between himself and the Senator to-day.

INSURANCE COMPANIES
THREATEN TO LEAVE.

Knoxville's Recent Big Fire Leads
Them To Demand Improvements
In Fire Department.

Knoxville, Tenn., Jan. 10.—[Special.]

It is given out that two and perhaps more prominent fire insurance companies are seriously considering withdrawing from the Knoxville field and canceling their policies that are now held here, or considerably reducing the face value of the policies in force here.

This, it is claimed, is due to the companies' alleged inefficient fire protection afforded by the city of Knoxville. It is cited that a similar action was taken a few years ago in Memphis, and this was followed by the city bettering the fire department and the restrictions were subsequently withdrawn and the companies re-entered the field.

Stricken With Paralysis.

Owingsville, Ky., Jan. 10.—Rev. Edgar Amos Kendell, aged about sixty years, one of the best-known ministers of the old school in this section, was stricken with paralysis at his home near Carrington, this county. One side is entirely useless and speech is affected. He is in a critical condition.

Spain is dead.

All gambling joints have been closed at Joplin, Mo.

The net earnings of the United States steel corporation for the year 1902 amounted to $132,602,000.

Daniel J. Hill, assistant secretary of state, has been appointed minister to Switzerland.

The city of Detroit, Mich., is going into the coal business and will supply the people at cost prices.

After a recess over the holidays, the authracite coal strike commission resumed its task of taking testimony on the 6th.

Near Joplin, Mo., in the eastern part of Jasper county, an 11-foot body of coal was struck at a depth of 40 feet, and the coal is of the finest quality.

Four persons lost their lives in a fire at Chicago which destroyed the Somerset hotel on Wabash avenue. The fire was caused from bed clothing igniting from a cigarette.

Carl Scholz, manager of the mining department of the Choctaw, is giving much attention to a project for increasing the output of the mines along the line of the Choctaw.

As a result of a collision between a passenger train and the rear end of a freight train on the Pennsylvania railroad at Cochrane station, just above Dubuque, seven men are dead and seven others injured.

The demand of railway men in the south and west for a 20 per cent increase in wages may result in trouble on some of the large systems. A number of roads have flatly refused to accede to the demands.

Cole Younger has applied to the Minnesota pardoning board for a complete pardon, in order that he might return to Missouri, his old home. The terms of his parole forbid him leaving the state of Minnesota.

Mrs. Amelia Rollo, of Palmyra, Wis., hanged her two children, Arthur, aged 3 years, and Clarence, aged 5, and then committed suicided by hanging herself. In a note written to a friend before the tragedy Mrs. Rollo said: "I am driven to it by gossips of Palmyra."

Citizens at Arcola, Ill., held up an Illinois Central freight train and confiscated a carload of coal. Active among the confiscators were the pastors of the Presbyterian and Free Methodist churches, the president of the bank and one policeman. Each load was weighed, and strict account kept, in the hope of making a satisfactory arrangement with the owners.

A decision of more than usual interest was recently rendered in the United States district court for the southern district of Illinois. An express messenger was indicted for the sale of liquor in prohibition territory. It was sought to convict on the ground that he delivered packages of liquor ordered in licensed territory, or in other words, the prosecution contended that the place of delivery should be held the place of sale. The court held that the express agent had no knowledge of the contents of the packages, hence could not be held as guilty of violating the federal liquor laws.

The census bureau report on the cotton ginned from the 1902 crop up to and including December 31 last is 9,311,835 bales, irrespective of shape or weight, equal to 8,005,-503, according to the commercial counting. The ginners' estimate is 1,057,771 bales. This is 90.2 per cent of the crop.

Capt. Marmaduke and his crew of Americans, who about six months ago took charge of a Colombian gunboat, have resigned.

The colored postmistress at Indianola, Miss., whose resignation caused the postmaster general to close the office at the above point, has left the community and declares under no circumstances will she accept a re-appointment. Both the woman and her husband bear a good reputation, and the objection to her as postmistress was on account of her color, it being contended that 90 per cent of the business of the office was contributed by whites.

Hon. W. J. Bryan, who has just returned from a tour of Mexico, declined to be interviewed by a reporter on the financial conditions of the above country.

At Oakdale, La., thieves broke into the Watkins railway office, blew the outer door of the safe off the hinges with gunpowder, and secured $4 and some express packages.

A result of a collision between a passenger train and the rear end of a freight train on the Monongahela division of the Pennsylvania railroad near Pittsburg, Pa., seven men were killed and five badly injured.

J. A. Traylor, manager of a mine near Eureka, Neb., was attacked by a crowd of miners, when he drew a pistol and killed three of them and wounded two others. The miners had deleared they would run Traylor out of the community.

Fire followed by an explosion at Hobart, Okla., caused a loss of $50,-000. The fire started in a hardware store where dynamite was kept. The force of the explosion was so great that towns thirty miles from Hobart reported the shock.

The president has directed the appointment of Capt. Louis B. Lawton, twenty-sixth infantry, to be major in the judge advocate general's department. Maj. Lawton was badly wounded while with Col. Liscum's column on the assault on Tien Tsin. His injury is permanent and he will be retired at once with his increased rank.

The bureau of insular affairs of the war department has prepared for publication a comparative statement showing that for the ten months ended October 31, 1902, the customs and revenues in the Philippine archipelago were $7,475,586, against $6,921,559 in 1900, and $3,-759,993 in 1899. The figures represent the total customs house receipts expressed in United States currency value.

Mr. Wilson, secretary of agriculture, has ordered printed 100,000 copies of the report made by Mr. W. D. Hunter, a specialist of the department, on the results of his investigations in Texas during the past year on the ravages of the cotton boll weevil. Mr. Hunter's report is the most complete that has ever been made upon this subject, and there is a great demand among cotton growers for copies of it.

The people all over the country are greatly aroused over the coal shortage. In many sections it is impossible to secure fuel at any price, and the extent of suffering is widespread.

It is understood President Roosevelt will shortly appoint Governor Taft to be associate justice of the supreme court to succeed Justice Shiras. Gen. Luke E. Wright, of Tennessee, is to succeed Mr. Taft as governor of the Philippines.

Miss Etta Alldridge, the 22-year-old daughter of the sheriff at Oneonta, Ala., liberated two prisoners during the absence of her father. She accompanied one of the prisoners, Mayherne Murphee, a young man charged with murder.

Because his brother refused to give him a cigarette paper Pink Grove, a young man living at Grove Park, Fla., plunged a knife into his heart, killing his brother instantly.

Congress will be asked to appropriate $100,000 for a fair exhibit at the St. Louis exposition.

D. K. Pearson, of Chicago, has given $50,000 to the endowment fund of Pomona College at Claremont, Col.

THE FREEMAN: AN ILLUSTRATED COLORED NEWSPAPER.
Governor Longino of Mississippi has issued a proclamation ordering that the lawlessness of white cops in Franklin, Lincoln, Amitea a D Pike counties cease. He offers a reward of $50 for the arrest and conviction of each individual participating in the outrages complained of, the total amount not to exceed an aggregate of $1 000 in each of the counties named. Governor Longino has since the day of his inauguration shown himself a brave and conscientious officer who deserves the admiration and gratitude of good people everywhere. We trust his proclamation may prove effective. Since the Governor's proclamation was issued a mass meeting was held in Brookhaven, Lincoln county, at which strong resolutions were adopted condemning whitecapping and commending the Governor's stand for law and order—Southwestern Christian Advocate Thus the good work is growing as is shown by the above. A strong, healthy sentiment against lawlessness promulgated by those who stand before the public will do much to correct the abuses of to day. The colored man will do much good in the matter if he will study the question from all sides and conduct himself in accordance. The social question is the most dangerous one before the American people, dangerous because of the wide divergence of the races as conceived in the minds by many and the individual nearness as seen through their walks of life. The strong law of sentiment must be obeyed until time or circumstances serve to modify it. Appealing from sentiment when crystalized to statute laws is but an appeal from Caesar to Caesar. Laws are nothing in themselves; they must have sympathy and support, without which it would be as well that they be not written. WHITE CAPS MURDER TWO NEGROES
Surrounded Their Cabin at Night and Riddled Their Victims With Buckshot.
Lewisburg, Tenn., Aug. 4.—Need more, a colored settlement, east of this city, was invaded by White Caps last night after midnight. Two negro men were called from their houses and when they attempted to escape from the back doors they were riddled with bullets and buckshot. The cause of the shooting is not known as neither had committed any crime. The White Caps were mostly mounted, but some were in buggies. The coroner's jury this morning brought in a verdict of death from an unknown mob.
john-hunter-lewisburg-1903-08-04.A10:
MOB OF WHITECAPS KILL TWO NEGROES
HUNTER IS DEAD AND MILLIKIN FATALLY WOUNDED—NO CAUSE IS KNOWN AS BOTH MEN BORE GOOD I.EPUTATION.
Nashville, August 4.—A special to the Banner says: One negro was killed and another fatally wounded by a band of whitecappers last night. There were fifteen or twenty in the mob, which made its appearance at the home of a negro preacher named John Millikin, and after gaining an entrance demanded a light. Millikin told his wife not to strike a match, but she did so, and at the same time Millikin made his exit through a back door. He was commanded to halt, but continued to run until brought down by a volley. Millikin died almost instantly and nine bullet holes were found in his body.

John Hunter, a son-in-law of Millikin, was made to accompany the mob on a fruitless search for another negro, and in an attempt to escape was fatally shot in the back. The wife of Millikin was struck over the head with a gun and painfully injured.

No cause is assigned for the killing as both Millikin and Hunter are said to have borne good reputations. The coroner's jury returned a verdict to the effect that the negroes were shot by a masked mob unknown to the jury. The work of the mob is strongly denounced by law-abiding people of the country. The mob is said to have been made up of young men or boys.

TWO NEGROES SLAIN.
Mob Kills Two Blacks Without Any Apparent Reason.
Nashville, Tenn., Aug. 5.—John Millikin, a negro preacher, was killed and John Hunter, his son-in-law, fatally wounded by a mob of unknown men in Needmore, a suburb of Lewisburg, late Monday night. No reason was assigned for the murders, as both men bore good reputations.

Needmore, which is in Marshall county, is inhabited almost exclusively by negroes. Between midnight and 1 o'clock a party of disguised men, variously estimated at from fifteen to thirty, appeared at the Millikin home, and, after opening the door, demanded a light. Millikin told his wife not to strike a match, but she did so. At the same time, as the little proof obtainable goes to show, Millikin made his exit thru a back door. He was called upon by the invaders to halt, but he continued to run until followed by a volley of shot, which brought him down and resulted in his immediate death.

John Hunter, son-in-law of Millikin, who was sleeping in the same house, was taken in charge by the marauders, who asked him where Dave Turner, another negro could be found. Upon replying that he did not know they forced him to go with them on a fruitless search of the premises and started away with him in their custody.

According to Hunter's statement, he suspected that he would be killed, and watching his chances, made a break for liberty, but was fired upon, a charge of shot entering the small of his back. He is in a dying condition.

The disguised men then left. Persons who saw them say that they were young men or boys, with a single exception.

From the meagre evidence obtainable no reason can be assigned for the killing of Millikin, who was a quiet, inoffensive negro, altho it is said that his reputation in some respects was not of the best, and that on Monday he had remarked to two or three different persons that he was not going to be killed.

Hunter also bore a good reputation, there being no charges against him for wrong doing. Nine bullet holes were found in Millikin's body, of which either of three or four would have caused his death. Millikin's wife was struck over the head with a gun and painfully injured.

Coroner Bowden summoned a jury of inquest which was sent to the scene and after viewing the remains and taking the statements obtainable, held a brief session, and rendered a verdict that the negroes were shot by a masked mob unknown to the jury.

PROVED AN ALIBI.
Otis Fowler Was in Nashville When Lewisburg Mob Did Its Work.
Special to the Herald.
Lewisburg, Aug. 6. — Otis Fowler, who was charged with participating in the white-cappers raid at Needmore Monday night, in which Green Milligan was killed and John Hunter was wounded, was tried this morning before Squires Hill and Coffman.
Only ten minutes was consumed in the trial and Fowler easily proved an alibi, the evidence showing that he was in Nashville at the time of the shooting.

john-mccray-peoria-1903-10-30.A3:
Men Armed with Winchesters and Revolvers and Ordered to Fire if Jail Was Attacked.
TWO VICTIMS OF BRUTAL NEGRO
WHITE WOMAN AND A NEGRESS ASSAULTED NEAR EAST ST. LOUIS.
Both Clubbed So Seriously They May Die-Supposed Perpetrator of the Crime Surrounded by a Posse.
PEORIA, June 24.—For a few hours last night it looked as if this city might have a lynching or a battle with a mob. Only the coolness and determination of the sheriff, deputies and police, armed with Winchesters and revolvers, prevented the summary execution of "Billy" McRay, a negro. It was not until about 1 o'clock this (Wednesday) morning that the danger had passed.

At 10 o'clock last night Detective William A. Murphy was killed by McRay, a negro desperado whom he was attempting to arrest at the corner of Water and Eaton streets. Murphy, armed with a warrant for McRay on the charge of burglary, approached the negro, who was standing on the corner, and informed him that he was under arrest. Without a moment's warning McRay drew a revolver and shot the officer in the breast. He then attempted to make his escape, but was caught by Detective Chadwick. Murphy was taken to the hospital, where he died within twenty minutes of the time he received the wound.

McRay was hurried to the city jail, and in less than an hour a mob numbering at least 1,000 men and boys, had assembled and made a demand on the chief of police for the prisoner. The chief refused to surrender the murderer. In the hope of attracting the attention of the mob the fire department was called out and made a run past the jail. The ruse partially succeeded, a large number of the crowd following the fire department. In the meantime the chief had ordered all the electric lights in the city to be turned out, and in the darkness McRay was hurriedly taken to the county jail. In a short time the mob discovered that it had been deceived and formed in front of the county jail. The entire police force of the city was called out in order to guard the jail. At that time (11:30 p. m.) the jail was surrounded and there were rumors from the lower end of the city, where the dead officer resided, that another mob was gathering with the intention of lynching the negro. The situation was then very critical.

Shortly before 1 o'clock this morning, however, the mob began to disperse, awed by the determined attitude of Sheriff Potter, who stationed a dozen deputies and police in front of the jail armed with revolvers and Winchesters. They were instructed to fire on the mob should any attempt to enter the jail be made. Inside the building twenty police were stationed.

While at the present time (1 a. m.) the mob still clamors for the negro it is evident that they lack a leader and the authorities are confident they will be able to cope with the situation.

MURDER AT PEORIA. Officer Shot Down by Desperado— Lynching of Criminal Narrowly Averted.
Detective William E. Murphy of Peoria was shot and killed on Tuesday evening in that city by John McCray, a colored desperado, whom the officer attempted to arrest for stealing coal.

Officer Murphy had several times visited Canton, and was known to many here.

The murder of the officer caused intense excitement and indignation in Peoria and for some hours a lynching was imminent.

The Herald-Transcript of Wednesday morning says:

The murder occurred at 9 o'clock, at the corner of Water and Fayette streets. Detectives Murphy and Chadwick left the central station shortly after 8 o'clock on information received that the man who committed the robbery, which was on Sanford street, where some men's clothes had been taken, would be found somewhere along the levee district. Later complaint was lodged against McCray for stealing coal, and Murphy was so informed.

Arriving on the scene without any preliminaries Detective Murphy tapped McCray on the shoulder, and told him to come with him. In a flash the desperate negro whipped a revolver from his pocket and fired point blank at the officer.

The shot went true and struck the officer squarely in the left side of the chest, just below the shoulder. It penetrated a vital organ which bled freely. Murphy sank to the ground while his fellow officer, Chadwick, forced McCray to surrender. Policeman Nichols, attracted by the firing, hastened to the scene and accompanied the injured man and his assailant to the jail.

Within less than half an hour after the negro was placed behind the bars and an angry mob surrounded the jail and swarmed through the city hall and offices swearing vengeance, and only lacking a leader to show them the way into what would probably have been the death of many of them. Dozens of stern officers under the strictest orders of the chief of police and the mayor, held the crowd in check and stood the jeering and hooting of the desperate and blood thirsty people. Running strong chances of having the man taken from them, if discovered, the murderer was hurried from the city jail to a more secure place in the county jail. After the crowd finally discovered that they had been outwitted they rushed to the jail, and it was not until 3 o'clock this morning that they quieted down in a measure and left for their homes.

McCray had been mixed up in several small burglaries and was out of the city for a time, on account of the police wanting him. His killing of Frank Scherer, a saloonkeeper on Water street, two years ago, will be recalled and that he was acquitted

of the charge by what was said to be perjury by his friends, who got him out of the scrape.

He will now have to stand trial for murder again, but he can not be brought up until the November term of the circuit court. In the meantime he will be closely guarded by officers in the county jail. From all appearances his chances now look to be for him getting the full extent of the law, and that without undue ceremony.

At 3 o'clock this morning, the mob which had held forth around the county jail since before midnight, had entirely dispersed and with the exception of a few scattered groups of men, who lingered on the street corners, there was nothing to tell that any unusual excitement had happened.

For a time during the night the scenes about the county jail were stirring and the yells of the enraged members of the crowd could be heard for many blocks. Some of them left the jail and congregating in other places about the city argued different methods of revenge, none of which, however, could be well enough formulated to induce them to carry out any of their plans. The determined front displayed by the sheriff's force aided by the police put a damper on the intentions of many who would otherwise have been prompted to rush into serious trouble.
john-mccray-peoria-1903-10-30.A10:
Lynching Averted.
Peoria, Ill., June 26.—A special grand jury was called yesterday to consider the case of John McCray, who shot Detective William E. Murphy, and a special term of court will be convened to try him. McCray is confined in the Galesburg jail for safe keeping. The mob did not appear last night, being convinced that McCray was gone.

Yesterday morning McCray was hanged in effigy in the court house square. The court house janitor cut down the figure at daylight. Three telegraph poles lashed together as a battering ram were found in the rear of the pall yard.
john-mccray-peoria-1903-10-30.A12:
NEGRO SPIRITED FROM PEORIA.
John McCray's Life Saved by Officers Taking Him to Galesburg for Safe Keeping.

Peoria, Ill., June 25.—John McCray, the colored desperado who killed Detective W. E. Murphy, was taken out of the county jail through a door in the rear shortly after noon Wednesday. A carriage was waiting, and Sheriff Potter, accompanied by two deputies and his prisoner, drove to Pottstown, boarding a Chicago, Burlington & Quincy train for Galesburg, where McCray will be imprisoned until the date of the trial.

In the early part of the evening a crowd gathered in front of the county jail, and it became evident that an attempt would be made to force an entrance. State's Attorney Teft and Circuit Judge Green addressed the crowd, telling them that a special grand jury would be summoned immediately; that the trial would be held as soon as possible. In order to convince the mob that McCray had been removed a committee composed of six members of the mob were permitted to search the building. During the morning several colored men, who were confined in jail for petty offenses, were removed to the workhouse in order that no mistake might be made in the event that the jail was broken into by a mob. After hearing the report of their committee that McCray was not in the jail the mob dispersed.
john-mccray-peoria-1903-10-30.A16:
M'CRAY READY FOR DEATH.
Condemned Man Greets News With Regret—Persists He Is Innocent.
Condemned Man Greets News With Regret—Persists He Is Innocent.

Peoria, Ill., Oct. 30.—Sheriff Potter yesterday afternoon informed John McCray, who was sentenced to be hanged today for the killing of Detective W. E. Murphy on June 23, of the reprieve for thirty days granted by Governor Yates. Before informing him Sheriff Potter made a final attempt to secure a confession from the negro, but he stoutly declared his innocence, and said his life had been lied away.

When the news of the respite was communicated to him, McCray said; "November 27. Well, I wish it was tomorrow, for I have made my peace with my God and am ready to die. Again I swear before my Maker that I did not kill Murphy."

Governor Yates' action in granting the respite is generally indorsed, as the attorneys for McCray filed affidavits that they were in possession of new evidence of his innocence that would be presented to the supreme court. The governor, under the law, could not refuse the application.
john-mccray-peoria-1903-10-30.A17:
JUDGE HITS YATES
Peoria Jurist Denounces Granting of Respite to McCrea.
PRESIDED AT NEGRO'S TRIAL
Says Governor's Acts Tend to Increase Spirit of Mob Law.
Peoria, Ill., Nov. 3.—"The present governor of the state of Illinois is, in my opinion, doing more than anything else, by this action, to increase the spirit of mob law; the very thing that, through his efforts, a number of citizens of Danville have been sentenced to the penitentiary for."

In this language Judge Theodore N. Green of the circuit bench arraigned Gov. Yates for granting a reprieve to John McCrea, the negro who murdered Detective William E. MURDERER'S DOOM John McCray Hanged at Peoria on Friday Morning, for Killing Detective Murphy. HE MADE NO CONFESSION Went to His Death Denying Act of Which He Paid the Penalty Upon the Gallows.
Peoria, Dec. 11.—John McCray, colored, was hanged here Friday morning.

The drop fell at exactly 9:05.

McCray had requested that he be hanged as early as possible.

He went to his death protesting that he was innocent.

He smiled as the cap was slipped over his head at the last moment. He was perhaps the coolest man at the execution.

The hanging was without sensational features. McCray was taken from his cell and led to the gallows, a few steps away. This had been erected in the west corridor of the jail. There were no steps to climb, and within a few seconds from the time that McCray left his cell he was on the little trap door through which he was to drop to eternity.

He looked about him for familiar faces.

Sheriff Potter asked: "Have you anything to say?"

McCray answered that he merely wished to do what he had done before—insist that he was innocent of the crime with which he was charged.

The colored preacher, Leonard, then offered a prayer.

"Glory to God," said McCray at one stage of the petition.

The cap was then pulled over his head. He smiled as the officers did it.

They stepped back, the trigger was pulled, and McCray went to his death.

At 9:20 Dr. Tolsor pronounced him dead.

The body was then taken down and turned over to the undertaker.

McCray will be buried in the Potter's field.

Only a few people were gathered in the street in front of the jail.

The witnesses to the execution were principally the reporters and outside sheriffs.

McCray was hanged for shooting Detective William E. Murphy, who attempted to arrest him. No one saw the shooting, but every circumstance indicated that it was McCray, and he was found guilty and sentenced to death.

HE FORESAW ROPE'S END Negro Chokes a Woman in Search of Cash. SHE IS AT HIS MERCY Discovered He Hires a Boat to Cross the River. MOB GETS AFTER HIM He Realizes His Fate and Prefers Drowning.
Kansas City, Sept. 4.—An unknown negro, caught in the act of strangling Mrs. Margaret Gerahn, a white woman, in her home at Armourdale, Kan., a suburb, this afternoon, escaped to the Kansas river, where he drowned himself rather than run the chances of being lynched by a crowd who had chased him to the bank of the stream. The woman was seriously hurt, but will recover.

Mrs. Gerahn is a widow, 45 years of age. Her husband, who was a packing house employe, and her son were drowned in the great June flood, and she lived alone. The negro, aged about 30, called at the house about noon, and entering, stealthily locked himself in. He surprised Mrs. Gerahn at her work and demanded her money. When she insisted that there was none about the house, the negro threatened to kill her, and seizing her by the throat, began choking her. She became unconscious, and he locked her in a closet. When she had revived he dragged her from the closet and upon her persistent refusal to tell him where she kept her money, the negro repeatedly choked her. Neighboring women broke into the house after Mrs. Gerahn had been at the power of the negro for three hours, and found him standing over the prostrate woman, sinking his fingers into her throat. The negro hurried from the house and ran to the Kansas river, two blocks distant, where he hired a boat and ordered the owner to row quickly to the Missouri shore. When the boat had reached mid-stream a crowd of excited men and boys had gathered at the bank and shouted to the owner of the boat to return to shore. He started to do so, when the negro stood up in the boat and with the remark, "I have lived too long to die at the end of a rope," dived into the water. He drowned before the spot could be reached, and his body disappeared.

A new pattern woven of the old strands, a new variation of the universal and eternal theme, a new play with the old, old motive—a new story of a man and a woman and the interlocking of their hearts forms the subject of "The Silver Poppy," by Arthur Stringer. It is a unique rendition, a version fresh with the perennial freshness of human passion, with an individuality to distinguish it from the infinitude of other versions.

One has not gone far with the story of John Hartley and his alluring Cordelia before reaching the verdict that it is an artful piece of fiction with subtle power, and the verdict is not weakened, but gradually and surely confirmed to the end. It is a sudden, solemnous spell which the author casts over the reader, and, once exerted, it is clinging and lasting. When John, the starving novice in letters, meets Cordelia, the newly celebrated novelist, at a studio gathering the touch of their hands awakes the reader's interest as with a spark; there is a suggestion of unusualness amid commonplaces, and this suggestion is ever present throughout the tale's development.

Cordelia Vaughn, a rare blend of deceit and sincerity, selfishness and self-sacrifice, of impulsiveness and cold deliberation, securely captures the reader's affections, beguiling him into a confidence which he is loath to surrender. Indeed, it is doubtful whether the average man will bring himself eventually to distrust and despise her. In all apparent honesty she sets her heart upon John Hartley—had she a purpose at the very outset? The question is difficult to answer, even when the whole story is known at the end. But, whether or no she sought his heart because she wished to make him her tool, certain it is that she made fair return of love; she gave him her own freely. The woman loved from the beginning, always, undeviatingly—with this reflection the reader may attempt to excuse his own overweening lenency toward her—love covers a multitude of the reader's sins.

She was ingenuous, she was intensely human in her frailty, and at times it was her very love for John that inspired her fraud upon him—he had the grace to give her full motives for that, even when he divined her under-motives and deceptions. If, as is sometimes asserted, the purpose of a novel is merely to tempt the fancy with a woman, Mr. Stringer has achieved conspicuous success.

Fatal Shooting Affray.
Last Saturday afternoon trouble broke out at the terminus of the logging road which extends out a few miles from Florenville, which re-resulted in the killing of four negroes by the name of Laurant, and the wounding of two others.

The story is that the trouble really started several days ago. P. H. Hansborough, who is general superintendant of the logging interests of the Poitevent & Favre Company, and a man of high standing in that settlement, keeps a store at the end of the log railroad. Some of the negroes about the place, including the Laurant boys, had made themselves more or less obnoxious for some time. A young man from Mississippi was a clerk in the Hansborough store. One of the Laurant boys became "fresh" with him and refused to address him in a respectful manner, carelessly calling him by his last name without any sign of courtesy. This was done two or three times, when the young Mississippi, tired of the insult, knocked the negro down with an axe handle.

This much is said to have happened in the store proper. The matter caused some excitement, and shortly after the black received a load of shot from some one in the neighborhood of the store, but it is not known from whom. The wound inflicted was not necessarily dangerous, but it started the feud.

For some time the negroes, as already stated, had grown sulky and impudent. They had secured firearms and it is even said that some of the younger ones had been practicing at a target range, often making insinuating remarks about what might happen in the Parker neighborhood if some of the whites said anything.

Saturday evening, it appears, the suspected trouble broke out in all its fury. Tiring of the insulting manner of the blacks, the leading white men of the settlement took thematter in their own hands and the immediate result was as above stated. The latest account was that a fusillade of shots followed the real encounter Saturday night. Three were killed outright and the fourth died before the officers reached the scene.

Deputy Sheriffs Hiram Cook and S. J. Talley were promptly on the scene, and found that quiet had been restored. They made one arrest, Jules Laurant, charged with assault and battery.

linton-linton-1903-07-13.A3:
RIOT FEARED AT LINTON.
pected There To-Day.

Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

TERRE HAUTE, Ind., July 12.—Governor Durbin to-day called up by telephone Alec Sandison to ask about conditions in Linton, and it is understood that it was with a view to some action to-morrow, when it is expected there will be another race conflict in that mining town. A circus which employs a large number of negroes is billed for Linton to-morrow. Sandison is the caterer who took a number of negro waiters to Linton last week for the Elks' banquet, and who was ordered to send the negroes out of town, which he did, with a mob of two thousand persons expediting the departure of the scared waiters.

Linton has not permitted negroes to live in the town since a coal company some years ago imported negro miners from Kentucky, who were afterward driven away. The Terre Haute Elks and Sandison say, however, that a negro baseball club played in Linton not long ago without the suggestion of trouble. It is said that one cause for the mob demonstration against the Terre Haute waiters was the fact that a large number of Linton men had been blackballed by the Elks.

Eugene Debs, in an interview, calls on the United Mine Workers to discipline their Linton men for the part taken in the Elks demonstration of mob violence. "The organization can do no less," he says. "It is appealing to the negroes of Kentucky and West Virginia mines to help fight its battles. At this very hour President Mitchell is in Kansas assuring the negroes that the miners' union is their friend and proposes to recognize them on terms of equality. The Linton affair is an utter repudiation of the union's professions, and if unrebuked the negroes will have no reason to regard the union in a friendly light." Negro miners are employed in the mines elsewhere in the State, and they are members of the United Mine Workers.
linton-linton-1903-07-13.A6:
NEGROES BARRED FROM TOWN.
Circus Employees Not Allowed to Enter Linton, Ind.—Miners Objected.
INDIANAPOLIS, July 13.—The people of Linton, a coal mining town of Green county, gave notice several days ago that the negroes who are attached to the Wallace circus must not enter the place. The show was billed there for to-day and the outlook was so threatening that Gov. Durbin called up the Sheriff by telephone this morning and suggested swearing in a large force of deputies. The Sheriff admitted that the feeling against the negroes is strong and promised to see that the peace of the town was preserved.

The Wallace company had received notice of the threats and when the train bearing the company reached Switz City, twenty miles from Linton all the negroes were ordered to stay there till the show was given at Linton and then to join the company at another place. This precaution saved trouble, as the people had determined that no negroes should enter the town.

The prejudice against the negroes is confined to the coal miners and their families and is said to have been caused by the employment of negroes in the mines several years ago, when the white men were on a strike. As soon as the strike was settled the negroes were all driven away and not a negro has been allowed in the town since.
linton-linton-1903-07-13.A7:
Troops Held in Readiness.
Governor Durbin received a telegram from B. E. Wallace, proprietor of Wallace's circus, stating that everything was quiet at Linton and that he feared no trouble of any kind during the day or evening. It had been anticipated, in view of the hostile demonstration made by the people of Linton against negroes from Terre Haute last week, that when Wallace's circus came to that place yesterday with a number of negro employes, trouble might occur. In order to avoid any such complications Mr. Wallace left sixty of his negroes at the last place he showed, with instructions to report at the next stop after Linton.

The Governor took the precautions to have the Terre Haute company of militia in readiness all day yesterday to proceed to Linton at a moment's notice. He kept his arrangements secret, however, and when he was asked last evening if the company had been under arms all day in case of an emergency call from Linton, he smiled and said:

"Well, I imagine it would not have been very hard, nor have taken much time, to find all the members of the company if they had been needed."
