NO TROUBLE AT LINTON
CIRCUS NEGROES HAD BEEN SIDE- TRACKED TO EFFINGHAM.
Durbin Had Troops Ready—First Arrest Made at Evansville—Refugees Make Trouble at Vincennes.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal. LINTON Ind July 13 Walk
Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

LINTON, Ind., July 13.—Wallace's show arrived in this place from Bedford Sunday morning and gave an exhibition this afternoon to a tremendous crowd. Nearly all the mines closed to-day in consequence, as it is the first opportunity the people have had to attend an animal show in Linton, owing to insufficient railroad facilities herefore.

Owing to the feeling here against the colored people, Mr. Wallace did not bring his negroes to Linton, but sent them on to Effingham, Ill., where the show will be tomorrow.
linton-linton-1903-07-13.A9: The town of Linton, in the state of Indiana, denied itself the pleasure of seeing a circus the other day. Linton, like most other mining towns, was all agog when it learned that the circus was coming, and young and old got their half-dollars handy to exchange for the pasteboards that would gain for them entrance into the big tent. Then the information got out that there were a number of negro employees with the circus. Linton, Ind., does not like the brother in black, and will not permit one to enter the incorporated limits. A delegation of Linton citizens met the circus twenty miles from town and asked the managers of it if it was true that there were negroes with the show. It was. The show people were told that the blacks could not enter Linton; that the circus would be welcome if it would leave its negroes outside the town, and pick them up afterwards. The show people explained that the colored help was necessary to making the performance come off smoothly; that the canvassmen, cooks, hostlers, drivers, waiters, etc., were essential to the running of the organization. But Linton was firm, so the circus had to skip the town. And yet the North reads the South lectures on its hostility to the colored man!
linton-linton-1903-07-13.A11:
Beats the Jim Crow.
The Columbia State says a year ago a white man was killed by a negro in Linton, Ind. Since that time no negroes have been allowed in Linton. On Monday the Wallace circus was billed in that town and the management was warned in advance that the 65 negroes connected with the show should not be brought to Lenton, so the negroes were taken to a town six miles south of Linton and left while the circus went on. A crowd met the train and several hundred men inspected the outfit to see that there were no negroes along. Special coaches were sent for the negroes left behind and this train was rnn up to Linton at night when the circus was ready to leave and as the train passed through the town the negroes crouched behind the seats to avoid danger. This mode of traveling in a northern State is a little worse than the Jim Crow cars down south, isn't it?

louis-hogan-oxon-hill-1903-07-04.A1:
DEATH RESULT OF ROW
LOUIS HOGAN, COLORED, THE VIC-TIM OF ASSAULT.
Three White Men Arrested, Given Preliminary Examination and Lodged in Marlboro' Jail.
The killing occurred on Oxon Hill road, not far from the saloon conducted by the McNeys at the cross roads, and in whose employ the dead youth was. Immediately following the crime the participants in the affair fled. Officers of the county were in pursuit of them all the night and yesterday morning about 6 o'clock Charles F. Osterman, a member of the Washington police force attached to No. 6 station, took into custody the three men who were later held by the coroner's jury as having knowledge of the crime. These men are Ernest Allen, Joseph Sansbury and Jesse Sansbury, all white, who reside with their people in small habitations near the District line, not far from Congress Heights.

Officer Osterman, who was at his home near the District line on sick leave, was requested by the law officials of the county to aid them in pursuing the alleged criminals. After being given a description of the men suspected the officer had but little difficulty in tracing them to their respective abodes, and he soon placed them in the custody of the Maryland authorities. Osterman, Constable John H. Webster and Deputy James Grimes accompanied the prisoners through the woods to Oxon Hill, where a coroner's jury sat the greater part of yesterday in hearing evidence, the outcome being the holding of the three suspects referred to for the October term of the court at Mariboro'.

Great Excitement Results.

The tragedy aroused residents of Oxon Hill district, particularly the colored citizens, to a higher pitch of excitement than has any occurrence in years. No violence was attempted, however. Nevertheless, the sentiment was freely expressed by the colored men that "The prisoners had better be taken away from here before night," and so the officers concluded to act upon the suggestion.

There is general evidence among those residents of Oxon Hill who were acquainted with Louis Hogan to show that he was regarded as an inoffensive youth and one who was never known to have been in any trouble. His father lives at Oxon Hill village and his mother resides at 1006 Loudoun place southeast.

Young Hogan had been in the employ of the McNeys for a month. Saturday night George Hatton, a colored citizen of Oxen Hill, gave a musical entertainment in a grove on Oxen Hill road, and a company of negroes assembled to attend. It was while the crowd was in the act of passing up the road to the place of entertainment that they came in clash with the white men, who were coming the other way, with the result stated.

Different stories concerning the killing have been told, one of them being that the Sansburys have had bad feeling toward the McNeys, and toward any one known to be in their employ, for several months, as the outcome of some difficulty in the saloon in which Benoni Sansbury, the elder, so it is alleged, was wostred, and in which, it is claimed, a pistol was used. One theory is that the Sansburys and their friends, recognizing Hogan as being employed by the McNeys, singled him out of the crowd of colored people as an object of attack. Rocks and stones of all kinds were freely used, some of the missiles striking houses in the neighborhood with terrific force, but the battle was suddenly ended by the cry: "They've killed Hogan."

Hogan had in the meantime fallen in a ditch, from where he was dragged dead. His body, it developed later, had the appearance of having been stamped upon in an outrageous manner. Dr. C. H. Parker of Oxen Hill pronounced him dead. Following the discovery that some one had been killed there was a general fleeing of all who had taken part in the fight. The officers of the county took up the trail, as stated, while Magistrate Waring and other citizens prepared for the holding of an inquest.

Jury Impaneled.

When the prisoners were taken to the scene of the crime by Officers Osterman, Webster and Grimes the following jury was impaneled by Judge Roberts: S. S. Adams, foreman; John Washington, Harry W. McKim, Guy Grimes, John D. Locker, Hugh Thompson, J. Alfred Butler, John C. Barrows, E. May, jr.; Silas Talbert and William Brown. Of these Washington, Locker, Thompson, Butler and Brown are colored.

The inquest was held in an unoccupied house to where the body had been removed. Dr. Parker described to the jury the injuries that had caused death, he having made an autopsy. The intestines and general appearance of the interior of the abdomen indicated that Hogan had been struck with a large missile at that point, and had been stamped upon as well. The principal wounds were at this point.

The other witnesses examined were John McNey, Edward McNey, sr.; Morris Cox, Richard Dement, Robert Busch, Amos Dean, Lemuel Jennifer, Robert Thompson, John A. Baden, Thomas R. McNey, John H. Webster, William Proctor, Harvey Talbott, Miss Addie Sansbury, George Allen, Richard Proctor and G. D. Simms. The general statements of the witnesses as to the meeting of the two bodies of men in the roadway agreed, as did their statements as to who threw the rocks. Some of them saw Hogan fall.

Miss Addie Sansbury, daughter of William Sansbury, who works at Glesboro' and lives in Oxon Hill, stated she was walking along the road with Joseph Sansbury just before the attack began. She ran to her home, nearby, when the tumult assumed dangerous proportions.

The prisoners were brought forward and examined. They admitted having taken part in the fractas, but only as a matter of self-defense, they said, and denied throwing any missiles. It was their claim that they had been accosted by the negroes while passing along the roadway with Miss Sansbury.

Jury's Decision Quickly Reached.

It required but a few minutes on the part of the jury to bring in a verdict holding the three men named. They were later placed in a wagon, and, accompanied by Constable Webster and others, were removed to jail at Marlboro'. Robert Proctor, Amos Dean and Robert Busch, the last named colored, were held in nominal bond as witnesses. The action of the jury was evidently pleasing to both white and colored residents.

The prisoners took their arrest coolly. Allen, whose mother is a sister of Benoni Sansbury, the father of Joseph Sansbury, is about twenty-one years old. His father was killed on Congress Heights several years ago by another man. Jesse Sansbury is twenty-four years old, and his mother is Mrs. Annie Sansbury. Joseph Sansbury is twenty-six. When arrested their clothing bore evidence of the owners' journey through woods, mud and water. They were arrested at Ernest Allen's house. All three are unmarried.

The body of the dead youth was removed last evening by his people from the inquest room. It was delivered to Undertaker George H. Mason of Hillsdale for burial, which will be made at Oxon Hill cemetery.
louis-hogan-oxon-hill-1903-07-04.A2:
Beaten to Death.
The body of John Hawkins, colored, thirty-six years old, was found at 6 o'clock yesterday morning in an outbuilding adjoining the barn of Edward McMay, at Oxon Hill, Md., opposite this city. Contusions all over the body indicated that the man had been kicked to death. Saturday there was a negro picnic about a mile from McMay's place, which Hawkins attended. On his way home Hawkins met Jesse Sansbury, who was walking with a young woman. Sansbury said Hawkins jostled him. Later Sansbury, his brother Joseph and Ernest Sellen attacked Hawkins with the result given above.
louis-hogan-oxon-hill-1903-07-04.A3:
The Oxon Hill Tragedy.
The Oxon Hill Tragedy.
To the Editor of The Evening Star:
In The Evening Star of July 6 there was published an account of a tragedy that occurred at Oxon Hill, Md. The facts stated in that account were not wholly true, in that it left the impression that the people engaged in the trouble attended the picnic given on that day by George Hatton. None of the parties had attended the picnic, and no trouble of any kind occurred there that day. Knowing your love for truth and your fairmindedness, I ask you if you will not publish this fact in justice to us. The boy Louis Hogan, who was murdered, was employed by Mr. McNey, who conducts a saloon at Oxon Hill, and the boy was knocked down and beaten in front of his place of business.
GEO. C. HATTON, Oxon Hill, Md.

The following is the report of the grand jury, which was discharged on Monday: To the Honorable, the Judges of the Circuit Court of Prince George's County:

We, the grand jurors for the October term of your Court, hereby respectfully report that we have been in session for 13 consecutive days and have examined 109 witnesses, have found 43 presentments, 43 indictments and have dismissed for various reasons 21 cases.

Fifteen constables have been before us, who generally report very few violations of law in their respective bailiwicks for our action. While from the evidence brought before us this peace and good order so reported is generally true, we feel in duty bound to report that in certain bailiwicks, where such good order is reported to be, the strongest evidence by reputable witnesses has been produced showing that open, constant and flagrant violations of the Sunday law against selling liquor and the law against gambling have been going on. It being the duty of constables to hunt up and bring to justice all violators of the law, it is anomalous and remarkable that nearly all the evidence, where presentments have been made in certain quarters, have come from private citizens alone, who wish to see the majesty of the law upheld and peace and order maintained in their respective neighborhoods. That being the case the inference is very plain that said constables are very neglectful of their sworn duty or
We have visited the jail and find the building and grounds in as neat and tidy condition as its crowded condition would justify. Evidence has been presented to us that while the food furnished the prisoners confined therein has at all times been ample in quantity, there have been times when its quality has been unfit for the maintenance of normal health in the prisoners.

A committee of our body has visited the Alms House, whose report is hereto annexed and is a part hereof.

Since we have been in session the State's Attorney has rendered us valuable aid and assistance, and all the officers of the Court have shown us great courtesy and consideration, for all of which we return our thanks.

We also thank the Court for the information, kindness and courtesy extended to us, and now, as we have fully examined into all matters laid before us, we respectfully ask to be discharged.

HENRY P. ARMSTRONG,

louis-hogan-oxon-hill-1903-07-04.A14:
THE GOVERNOR'S BUSY DAY
RECEIVES MANY REQUESTS FOR CLEMENCY.
He Refuses to Discuss a Serious Case of Criminal Assault on Mrs. Emma Florijanek.
FIXES DATE OF EXECUTION OF SYDNEY JOHNSON.
Serious thought was given by Governor Warfield today relative to executive clemency in a variety of cases. He was asked for pardons in a number of cases, but refused to exercise the power vested in him to any great extent. Owing to the fact that he had been detained in Baltimore on other business yesterday his executive session was held today. He arrived at the Executive Department early and found a number of persons waiting to see him.

A case of considerable interest which came before him was that of Sydney Johnson, colored, of Allegany county, who had shot and killed two other men in a Cumberland saloon. He was found guilty and was sentenced to be hanged. The date of his execution was set for Friday, January 27, and it was hoped to have the sentence commuted. Mr. Arch Young, of Cumberland made a strong plea in behalf of the youth, stating that the affair was one in which fear was the influence which prompted the young man to fire the fatal shots. Governor Warfield refused to interfere in the matter and the sentence of the Court will be carried out on the day mentioned.

Another case of capital punishment is that of Edward Cassidy, colored, who was convicted of a criminal assault on September 17 last on the person of Mrs. Emmia Florijanek. The Governor stated that this was a case wherein he would absolutely refuse to exercise executive clemency. He said that offenses of this kind should be dealt with speedily and surely and if that was done the danger and excuse of lynchings would be eliminated. He ordered that the man be hanged on December 23, the original time set by him.

A pardon was granted Ernest Allen, of Prince George county, charged with manslaughter. It was shown that the evidence was of a very conflicting nature and that there was much doubt as to the guilt of the young man.

The Governor commuted the sentence in the case of Georgianna Driver, of Howard county, who killed an infant child of her mistress by pouring concentrated lye down its throat. The testimony was very conclusive to the effect that the woman was weak minded and as not morally responsible, although she is not insane.

Willie Herbert, colored, of Baltimore, asked the Governor to remit to her a fine of $25 which had been assessed by a Baltimore justice. She was found guilty of the heinous offense of using for her house bottles which belonged to a bottling company. The matter was laid over for further consideration.

Affidavits of great length and convincing facts were presented by J. Frank Turner, of Easton, in the application for pardon of Madison W. Wright, of Denton. He was convicted of a criminal assault on his wife's sister seven years ago and sentenced to 21 years in the penitentiary. The facts produced today throw a different light on the matter and will be given further consideration by the Governor at a later hearing.

The Governor has appointed John C. Sheriff, of Prince George's county, Judge of the Orphans' Court of that county, vice his father, D. T. Sheriff, deceased. Mr. Sheriff is highly recommended as a young man of intelligence and ability and is well qualified for the place.

The Governor has designated Judge R. Irving Bowie as Chief Judge of the Ophans'r Court of Prince George's county, vice D. T. Sheriff, deceased.

In the case of James Upshur, colored, convicted and sentenced to jail for six months for assaulting and striking Charles Walton, which was advertised for final consideration today, was taken up by the Governor and he decided upon the recommendation of Justices Grannan, Packard and Goldman, who, at his request, reviewed the case and declined to extend executive clemency.

The Governor pardoned and remitted the fine imposed upon Howard Chew on November 6, 1904, by Justice Loden, of Baltimore city for assaulting Charles Beatty and sentenced to 60 days in jail and fined $10. This case is one which was thoroughly investigated by a committee of justices of the peace, who favorably reported the case for executive clemency.

lufkin-lufkin-1903-08.A1: The Lufkin commercial club has taken strong action against lawlessness in that town and offers rewards for recent offenders.
lufkin-lufkin-1903-08.A2:
Good for Lufkin!
The other day two negro brakemen employed by the Houston, East and West Texas Railroad were taken by a mob from a caboose in Lufkin, Tex., and whipped severely. Invigorated by the exercise, the mob returned to the car and fired several shots into it, just missing the conductor. The members of the Commercial Club and other citizens of Lufkin met, condemned the proceedings of the mob and offered a reward for the arrest and conviction of the rioters. One of the resolutions passed at this meeting is especially commendable:

"In anticipation of a repetition of such conduct, we pledge ourselves to stand ready, and do hereby pledge ourselves, to a prompt and speedy punishment of any further outrageous conduct toward the colored people of this town and county."

This shows sound business sense, as well as humane feeling. It is to the commercial advantage of Lufkin to be known as an orderly place. Southern labor being mainly negro labor, no Southern town can afford to have colored laborers interfered with or injured by mobs. It is essential to Southern property and must be protected.

Some Americans have a way of explaining or excusing anything strange or repellant which the tourist may observe in their land, by saying deprecatingly, "'Tis a custom of the country (Costumbres del pais). macon-macon-1903-01-03.A1:
MESSENGER BOYS STRIKE.
Those at Macon Didn't Like Reductions in Their Pay. Macon. Jan. 2.—Six messenger boys
tions in Their Pay.

Macon, Jan. 2.—Six messenger boys at the Western Union office have been on a strike to-day, leaving only 7 to do the work of the office. Wages have been reduced from 2 cents to one and one-half cents per message. Manager Jackson says that if he cannot get enough white boys he will hire negroes to deliver telegrams.

There were ten boys on strike last night, but three of the number came back this morning. The strikers are abusing other boys who are at work and have threatened to do them violence. Manager Jackson frightened them away by saying that he would call the police if they did not go away from the back door.

Ben Mapp a boy about 7 years old, thinking that Clerk Palmer was to be blamed for the trouble, dared that gentleman, who weighs about 200 pounds, to come out in the alley and fight it out.

Manager Jackson says that he thinks that the boys will be able to make up the reduction by carrying packages and other articles, which will be allowable since the District Messenger Service now employs the boys and does the delivery business of the Western Union Company.
macon-macon-1903-01-03.A2:
WESTERN UNION PUTS IN NEGROES AT MACON.
White Boys Went Out on a Strike Because of Reduction. Mecon Jan 3-Fourteen negroes
Macon, Jan. 3.—Fourteen negroes have taken the places of the white messenger boys at the Western Union office.

The white boys have organized a union, and say that they will not go to work again unless they get the same wages as formerly. Friday night they were told that they would get 1½ cents, instead of 2 cents, for handling telegrams. All but three determined not to begin work, and these quit this morning. In a few hours negroes were in their places. The white boys declare that they will mob the negroes.

Business men say that the employment of negroes will hurt the patronage of the company.
macon-macon-1903-01-03.A3:
MACON MEN PETITION FOR MESSENGERS.
Maxwell is Trying to Straighten Matters Out. Macon Jan 5 Toodyay
Macon, Jan. 5.—To-day a petition signed by several hundred of its principal patrons in the city, was presented to Manager Jackson of the Western Union office, asking that the negro messenger boys be discharged and the white boys reinstated. The petition was promptly forwarded to Supt. B. F. Dillon at Jacksonville. The management here will wait to hear what he has to say in the matter.

Assistant Superintendent Maxwell of Savannah arrived here this morning, having come to help Manager Jackson straighten out the situation. He says that neither Macon nor the boys have been discriminated against. He mentioned Savannah, Atlanta, Tampa and Jacksonville among the places where negroes are employed without protest. He said that as to the boys they would be able to make as much at the very beginning and more after a while by the arrangement with the District Messenger Service.

He says that the office did not wish to employ negroes and did so under compulsion in order to deliver telegrams and discharge its obligations to the public. It has stated that those seen by him were satisfied with this explanation, and that he would, visit every signer of the petition to settle the question without hard feeling.

martin-willis-dekalb-1903-10-24.A2:
Serious Cutting Affray.
Friday evening last, on the place of Mr. Hute Shumate, about eleven miles northwest of DeKalb, occurred an affray which may result in the death of three men, from wounds inflicted and the hanging of the fourth.

From what we have been able to learn, it seems that Ben and Willis Martin (colored), father and son, have been in the habit of leaving down the bars in the fence on Mr. Shumate's place, and he had remonstrated with them about it a number of times. Friday evening Mr. Shumate and his son Eli found the fences down again and, the negroes being in a nearby field, spoke to them about it. The latter were impudent and a fight followed, in which Mr. Shumate and Ben Martin were so badly cut that they are not expected to recover, young Eli Shumate was dangerously if not fatally cut and Willis Martin received some slight cuts.

The latter was placed in jail at DeKalb Saturday, and that night a crowd of masked men gathered in the town with the evident intention of lynching the prisoner. Sheriff Hull had been warned in time, however, and had a large force of special deputies to guard the jail, upon learning which the mob dispersed.

To prevent further trouble Sheriff Hull, accompanied by Mr. A. A. Overstreet, on Sunday conveyed Willis Martin to Macon, where he was placed in jail for safe keeping.—Kemper Herald.

mrs-foster-chanute-1903-08-12.A1:
NEAR TO RACE WAR.
Crowd of 300 Whites Carrying Clubs Out at Chanute.
Chanute, Kan., Aug. 13.—The Tribune says:

The prospective invasion of a negro family into the quiet precinct of the new Evergreen park second addition was the cause of a very large mass meeting of the residents last night. They met three hundred strong around the partially completed foundation of the negro home and discussed the question of allowing a colored family to settle in the new addition. Thus far there are no negroes residing in that part of the Fourth ward and the Evergreen residents seem to think that other than colored neighbors should occupy homes there, fearing if one colored family were allowed to build others would follow the example. In fact a real estate firm had already sold a second lot to a negro, who the leaders of the mob understood, intended building there at once. The posse seemed inclined to resort to violence if necessary to prevent such an occurrence.

Discussion over the vexed question waxed eloquent and methods of procedure were suggested by the score. Those assembled were unarmed except for the most part peaceably inclined, though firmly determined to thwart any attempt of the negroes to settle in that vicinity. A large number of the crowd favored purchasing the lots of the negroes by popular subscription and then disposing of them in the most satisfactory manner possible. Others argued that while such a method would rid them of the prospective residents and relieve the present stringency, it would only be establishing a bad precedent and would furnish them no protection against later immigrants. It was finally agreed to appoint a committee to visit Mrs. Foster, the colored lady building the house, and attempt to dissuade her from building.. If the committee was not successful in its efforts then the residents would assemble and tear down the negro dwelling. After having arrived at this conclusion the mob disbanded. It was nearly midnight, however, and the mixed crowd of three hundred laborers, some carrying heavy clubs, looked singularly sinister as it dispersed.

otto-mischke-fremont-1903-05-09.A1:
MOB READY WITH ROPE
Negro Murderers in Jail at Fremont, O., in Danger of Being Lynched.
Fremont, O., May 9.—A serious conflict, the outcome of labor troubles in this city, occurred here late tonight. Otto Mischke, 20 years old, was shot and killed and Albert Gummell fatally wounded, the shooting being done by a gang of colored nonunion men, three of whom are now in jail. The police are searching for the others.

A party had taken place at the Gummell home, and as the guests were homeward bound they met a crowd of colored men. Remarks passed at which the negroes took offense and the shooting followed, the colored men starting the shooting.

Albert Gummell was shot in the leg and body, and his son, R. C. Gummell, was shot in the leg.

Otto Mischke, who came to the rescue, was shot through the heart and instantly killed.

The police soon arrested three colored men, all claiming Cleveland as their home. Although late when the murder was committed the news soon spread, and great excitement was created, and a mob was soon formed and started for the jail. All but three of the negroes in the party escaped.

William Kimbro is the man who is believed to have killed Mischke, he having partially made a confession, it is said.

Revolvers which had recently been discharged and reloaded were found on the persons of the three arrested negroes.

Cleveland, May 10. 2:10 a.m.—A bulletin just received from Fremont says the mob still surrounds the jail, clamoring for the prisoners. A false alarm of fire has been turned in with the hope of scattering the crowd.

The police are using every effort to prevent the prisoners falling into the hands of the mob, and at this hour express the hope of being able to do so.
otto-mischke-fremont-1903-05-09.A6:
SHOT IN A RACE CLASH.
White Man Killed and Another Wounded in Fremont, Ohio.
FREMONT, Ohio, May 10.—As a result of a clash between some negroes and whites here about midnight last night, Otto Miscke, white, is dead, and Gilbert Gommell, white, received a bullet in his thigh. Three negroes, Wheeler Kimber, Lorenzo Martin and Walter Shatton, are in jail charged with murder.

Ralph Gommell was going home from a party at his father's house, accompanied by his wife and baby. As he passed a crowd of negroes he made a remark, to which they replied. Gommell threw a stone, striking Kimber on the head.

The negroes then drew revolvers and began firing. Albert Gommell, father of Ralph, and Otto Miscke ran out of the house. Miscke received a bullet in his side and staggered back into the house, falling dead at the door, and Gommell received a bullet in the thigh.

The police were summoned and arrested the negroes, who had taken refuge in a house. When the news of the killing became known, a crowd of 200 men went to the jail and demanded the men. Not having a leader, the crowd dispersed. This afternoon the men were taken to Newark jail for safety.
otto-mischke-fremont-1903-05-09.A7:
WAS NO LYNCHING.
Sheriff at Fremont Succeeded in Averting It. Fremont. O. May 10-Mob violence
Sheriff at Fremont Succeeded in Averting It.

Fremont, O., May 10.—Mob violence, which was threatened in this city last night as the result of the alleged killing of Otto Mischke by one of three negroes, subsided at 4 o'clock this morning. The three negroes who are charged with the crime are securely locked in the county jail at Norwalk, and the excitement that was rampant for several hours last night has about subsided.

From 1 o'clock until 4 o'clock Sunday morning, the jail building was surrounded by the angry crowd calling upon Sheriff Mason to deliver the prisoners. For an hour or more the sheriff stood on the front steps of his residence and admonished the threatening crowd to be careful and quiet, and not commit an act that would forever shame Fremont in the eyes of the world. Sheriff Mason said he had taken an oath to do his official duty, and do it he would, and he said he would shoot the first man who made an attempt to break down the jail door and enter the building.

For fear of further trouble during the day and to-night, Mayor Engler ordered every saloon in the city closed.

The negroes gave their names as Wheeler Kimbro, Walter Stratton and Lorenzo Martin. Martin and Stratton had loaded revolvers in their possession.

To-day's story of the tragedy is to the effect that the negroes who were in the street were offended at a question of Mrs. Albert Gommel as to who they were. Mrs. Gommel was on her way home with her husband and children. Mische, the victim of the bullet, was living at the Gommel House, which was in the vicinity of the affray, and when he came to the door to see what the loud talk was about, a bullet struck him in the stomach, inflicting a fatal wound.
otto-mischke-fremont-1903-05-09.A9:
SHERIFF SAVES THREE NEGROES FROM MOB
CLEVELAND, May 11.—In order to prevent the lynching of the three negroes accused of shooting and killing Otto Lischke and severely wounding Albert and R. C. Gummel, the prisoners were removed from the jail at Fremont and taken to Norwalk for safety. The Gummels had entertained friends, and some of the guests on their way home met a crowd of negroes. The whites and negroes tried to push each other off the sidewalk. In the scuffle revolvers were drawn by the negroes, who fired a volley at the white men.
otto-mischke-fremont-1903-05-09.A15:
TROOPS NOT YET NEEDED.
Columbus, O., May 12.—A request from the sheriff of Sandusky county for troops to guard the workmen at the Clauss Shear company's plant at Fremont, was refused today by Governor Nash, who held that there was no emergency warranting the calling out of the militia. The feeling growing out of the strike at the Clauss plant has been very bitter since the killing of Otto Mischke last Saturday night, which resulted in the arrest of three colored non-union men employed at the plant.
otto-mischke-fremont-1903-05-09.A21:
THE FREMONT RIOT
So many conflicting stories have been sent broadcast over the country relative to the riot in Fremont, O., last Saturday night, resultant from a strike of the employees of the Clauss shear works, that it is about time for the truth to have a hearing. The facts are, that a number of Afro-Americans from Cleveland and other northern Ohio points were employed to take strikers' places. Some did not know that this was to be the case until almost on their arrival in Fremont. Others were made acquainted with the situation before arrival. As is usually the case, a mob consisting of strikers and sympathizers assaulted three young Afro-Americans by the names of Stratton, Kimbro and Martin, injuring severely at least one of them. They retaliated, shooting into the crowd and killing at least one striker and injuring others. This, of course, was in self-defense, because their lives were being jeopardized. As is usually the case, the Afro-Americans were arrested and taken to the jail at Norwalk, O., after a very weak attempt was made by two or three foolish admirers of the southern way of doing such things—lynching. They did not tarry long near the Fremont jail, because the sheriff told them in very plain language that he would kill anyone who approached any nearer the jail door. This, of course, settled the matter as far as the cowards were concerned. The following dispatches to the daily papers of Wednesday and Thursday are self-explanatory: Norwalk, O., May 12.—The case of Stratton, Kimbro and Martin, the three young colored men brought to Norwalk from Fremont Sunday, will be investigated by the Sandusky county grand jury to-morrow. This plan will obviate the necessity of taking the prisoners to Fremont for a preliminary examination before a magistrate and consequently they will probably be kept in jail in Norwalk until they are placed on trial in the common pleas court. Their attorneys will probably ask for a change of venue, so that it is probable that the trials will take place in Huron county. The three prisoners, acting upon the advice of their attorneys, refuse to talk about the shooting affair in Fremont, merely saying that the published accounts are untrue, that the "other side" was more to blame than they were and that the truth will become known at the proper time. They refuse to talk to anyone on any subject relative

A large number of colored people, men, women and children, passed through Norwalk late yesterday afternoon from Fremont en route to Oberlin and other places. The number included not only those connected with the Clauss shear works, but also those who had been residents of Fremont for many years. Fremont, O., May 13.—A country churchyard could not have been more quiet or more orderly than Fremont was to-day. The militia was not needed, there being no disturbances. No demonstration was made near the Clauss factory other than the assembling of a large crowd expecting to see trouble when the management attempted to start the works. No attempt was made by sympathizers, either by word or force, to prevent any man who desired from entering the factory. Only a few entered, not sufficient to operate the works. The settlement rumors are still in circulation, but although overtures have been made, as yet the agreement has not been made. It is predicted that the settlement will come Thursday. Three men are now charged with the murder of Otto Mischke. They are Wheeler Kimbro, Lorenzo Martin and Charles Stratton, locked up Saturday night. Richard Pettiford and son Will were placed under arrest to-day at Berlin Heights while en route to Bellevue to give themselves up. The first three had their hearing at Bellevue, waived examination, and were bound over without bail for first degree murder. The hearing of the Pettifords is set for Saturday, but in the meantime it is thought they will be indicted either as principals or accessories to the crime. The five colored men were returned to the Norwalk
Bellevue, waived examination, and were bound over without bail for first degree murder. The hearing of the Pettifords is set for Saturday, but in the meantime it is thought they will be indicted either as principals or accessories to the crime. The five colored men were returned to the Norwalk jail. To-day the grand jury examined some 30 witnesses investigating the crime, and has about completed hearing testimony. A report will be made Friday. This evening everything in the city is absolutely quiet, and not a single incident of any moment is transpiring, the city seemingly having settled down to its normal state again, awaiting the settlement developments. Sheriff Mason is receiving hundreds of telegrams, letters and newspaper editorials congratulating him upon the brave stand he took when he faced the angry mob Sat...rday night last.
otto-mischke-fremont-1903-05-09.A23:
Strikers Indicted for Murder.
FREMONT, O., May 18.—Indictments for murder were returned this afternoon by the grand jury against Wheeler Kimbro, Lorenzo Martin, Walter Stratton, Richard Pettiford and William Pettiford, all colored. They are charged with the murder of Otto Mischke, who was killed by a bullet wound in the stomach. The Pettifords are named as accessories to the crime in that they were advisers.

WISH HIM SUCCESS.

Lots of People Want Sir Thomas to Lift the Cup.

Glen Summit, Pa., Aug. 1.—If the greetings Sir Thomas Lipton received from the crowds at stations where his special train stopped are an index, about half the people of Pennsylvania will be glad to see him lift the cup. "Wish you success" was the greeting at nearly every stop.

Easton, Pa., Aug. 1.—Several persons who recognizer Sir Thomas Lipton's private Shamrock flag among the decorations of the Lehigh Valley special gathered about the train in the Jersey City station and cheered Sir Thomas heartily. At Newark a crowd of 300 people greeted sir Thomas with cheers and waving handkerchiefs.

ORDERS FOR ARMS.

Chinese Province is Getting Ready for a Fight.

Pekin, Aug. 1.-Yuan Shai Kai, the Viceroy of Chi Li province is said to be placing large orders for arms in anticipation of the expiration of the prohibition of their importation into China, which will occur this month. He has ordered from Japan 23,00 rifles and forty-eight field pieces, and from Germany a number of machine guns.

Two thousand soldiers from Moscow have arrived at Port Arthur, and 14,000 more are reported to be en route.

CHOATE IS SPEAKER.

Cecil Rhodes' Bequest Wipes Our Provincial Spirit.

Provincial Spirit.
London, Aug. 1.—United States Ambassador Choate delivered the inaugural address at the university extension summer meeting at Oxford today to an audience of 1,300 persons. In the course of his address Mr. Choate said that the bequest of Cecil Rhodes providing scholarships for American students at Oxford would forever wipe out any provincial spirit which still existed and establish an endless chain of intercourse and sympathy.

FEARED A LYNCHING.

Sheriff Would Not Receive a Prisoner Until So Ordered.

Until Bo Ordered.

Vincennes, Ind., Aug. 1.—Sheriff Shake and Deputy Elliott of Oiney, Ill., brought Cyrus Beltman here tonight. They said that during a street fair at Oiney this evening Beltman had shot and killed Frank Price, a saloon keeper, and that they feared a lynching might follow. FATAL TO THE ACT.

Eight-Hour Law Cannot Be Submitted to Voters.

Helena, Aug. 1. According to W. J. McHaffle, who is printing the journals of the recent legislative assembly, house bill 55, under the provisions of which the eight-hour law was to be submitted to the electors of the state as a constitutional amendment, was omitted from the journal of the house. Authorities hold that such an omission is fatal to the act and the people of the state will not be given an opportunity to vote upon the proposed constitutional amendment.

RAIN WAS GENERAL.

Nebraska Had a Fine Fall of Moisture Yesterday.

Lincoln, Neb., Aug. 1—Reports from nearly every section of the state show that the rain of last night and today was very general. At a number of points the storm was severe, the worst four years at Franklin, where a number of houses were struck by lightning, bottoms flooded and bridges washed out. Some stock was killed. Patriots in Cuba Figure Their Services Above $80,000,000.

Havana, Aug. 1—The total of the claims of the persons listed as revolutionary soldiers and as civilians entitled to pay for services rendered during the recent revolution in Cuba is $1,889,000. The claims will be reduced by the auditing commission, and some will doubtless be disallowed.

Stand Collapses and Thirty People Are Injured. London, Aug. 1. As a result of the collapse of a grandstand at Perth, Scotland, during a cricket match today, thirty people were more or less injured, but there were no fatalities. HAD FEAR OF LYNC HING.
Sheriff Spirits a Negro Murderer Out of Larned.
Larned, Kas., Aug. 3.—This city was the scene of a sensational murder Saturday evening at 6 o'clock, when R. B. Williams, a negro tailor, shot and instantly killed Clyde Langdon, a young white man, of this place. The scene of the murder was at Williams' tailor shop, in the city building, where Langdon had gone to get a suit of clothes, which he had left with the negro to be pressed. The clothes were not ready and Langdon insisted that they be returned to him at once. Some words followed, when suddenly the negro whipped out a revolver and emptied its contents at the young man. Four of the shots took effect, two of them being fired after Langdon had fallen. Two of the shots struck vital parts, one entering the top of the head and ranging downward through the brain into the mouth, and the other entering the right shoulder and entering the region of the heart. Another shot penetrated the jugular vein. Langdon died within a few minutes without regaining consciousness.

The negro was immediately arrested and taken to the county jail. A mob formed within a few minutes and there was strong talk of lynching, but before any demonstration was made it was discovered that Sheriff McCoy had spirited his prisoner away on an east bound train which was just leaving the Santa Fe depot Langdon was a well known young man, who had been connected with one of the city restaurants for some months. He came here from Topeka.

IS BACK IN LARNED.
The Return of the Negro Who Might Have Been Lynched.
Larned, Aug. 4.—R. B. Williams, the negro tailor who shot and killed Clyde Langdon, a young white man at this place Saturday evening, was brought back here Monday from Hutchinson, where he had been taken for safe keeping. There was no demonstration, although a large crowd followed the prisoner to the jail.

The testimony at the coroner's inquest showed that young Langdon was at the negro's tailor shop several times during the day trying to get some clothes on which he had made part payment. The last time he applied with a pistol and demanded his money back, at the same time pointing the weapon full at Williams. The latter instantly grabbed a pistol which lay on his work table concealed under some cloth, and began firing. He will be given a preliminary hearing today.

SHOT IN SELF DEFENSE

Larned Negro Is Justified for His Shooting.

CORONERS JURY ACQUIT

Langdon Is Said to Have Drawn a Revolver.
Larned, Kan., Aug. 3.—The coroner's inquest over the body of Clyde Longdon, the young man who was shot and fatally wounded by R. B. Williams, the negro tailor, found from the evidence that Williams did the shooting in self-defense. The three witnesses all testify practically to the same story, that Longdon went to the tailor shop and demanded some money that he had advanced on a suit of clothes. Upon being refused this, he drew a revolver on Williams to force him to give up the money. Williams produced a gun from under some clothes that were near and began firing on Longdon. Williams fired five shots, four of which took effect. Great excitement was caused by the shooting, and until the facts were learned there was much talk of raising a mob and lynching the negro.

The officers, anticipating trouble, took Williams from the jail to the railroad junction east of town, where they boarded east-bound passenger train No. 8, with their prisoner, and took him to Hutchinson for safe-keeping.

sherman-sherman-1903-04.A1:
A Texas Sheriff.
A tall, wiry man, with a trailing moustache, good humored eyes and a pleasantly modulated voice, sat in the gallery of the Binkley House at Sherman. He is the sheriff of Grayson county—Lee McAfee, who has just made himself famous by standing out successfully against a mob. Lee McAfee faced a thousand angry Texans and saved a negro from summary vengeance. If ever a wretch deserved quick death this one did. He had assaulted the woman, and in carrying out his purpose had knocked the husband senseless and had beaten the children nearly to death. The brute was caught with his bloody clothes upon him.

Armed with shotguns and Winchester, the people marched to the jail and demanded the prisoner. McAfee looked into the desperate faces and shook his head. He did not doubt that the negro deserved death, but it was his duty to hold the negro for the court, and he would try to do it, even if he died in the attempt. The mob backed down before as fine an exhibition of courage as the state of Texas ever saw. And that is saying a great deal. At the hearing of the case the sheriff escorted the negro to and from the court room with a picked band of deputies. The mob stood waiting, rope in hand; !but the leader, who was a match for the dauntless sheriff, was not there. When the examination had brought out the whole revolting story, the mob at once moved to the jail and demanded the surrender. McAfee made the crowd a little talk.

"I see before me," he said, "men who voted for me with the understanding I was to perform all of the duties of sheriff of Grayson county. I took the oath to perform those duties and I gave bond to do it. I conceive it to be my duty to protect this prisoner, and I am going to do it though it cost me my life and the life of every deputy I have. All I desire is that this prisoner shall get a legal trial before twelve citizens. I propose to see that he gets it. Then if you say hang him, I'll hang him. I am willing he shall be hanged, but he must be hanged legally."

The mob stood awhile looking into that resolute face, and Texans though they were, they turned away. The cause was least worthy, but the majesty of the law was vindicated magnificently.—St. Louis Globe-Democrat.

ATTEMPT TO POISON FAMILY.
Negro Tries to Kill Matthew Crossby's Family, Living Near Brewton.
Montgomery, August 24.—A special to the Advertiser from Brewton, Ala., says:

An attempt to poison the entire family of Matthew Crossley, a prosperous farmer residing seven miles southwest of Brewton, was made today by a negro farm hand named Tom Fifer. The water bucket was heavily dosed with strychnine. Miss Crossley, a daughter, was the first member of the family to partake, and was taken violently ill. Fifer then assaulted Crossley with a rock, inflicting severe wounds, but finally escaped. Physicians say those who drank the water will recover.

Great indignation is felt against Fifer and threats of lynching are made.

DASTARDLY ATTEMPT
NEGRO BOY PUTS STRYCHNINE IN WATER BUCKET.
Tried to Poison Family of Matthew Crossley-Before Poison Took Effect He Attacked Crossley With a Stone.
Brewton, Aug. 24.—(Special.)—A dastardly attempt at poisoning the family of Matthew Crossley, a prosperous farmer residing seven miles southwest of Brewton, was made at an early hour this morning by a colored boy named Tom Fifer, aged about 20 years, who had been in Crossley's employ several months. The water bucket was dosed with strychnine.

Miss Crossley, a daughter, was the first member of the family to partake. The negro in the meantime pretended that a mule was sick. Mr. Crossley went to the lot to see after the welfare of the animal, when he was assaulted by Fifer with a rock, inflicting serious wounds on his head and breast. Crossley attempted to resist the assault, but the negro leaped a fence and has not been seen since.

Physilicans have been attending the victims today and is thought they will all recover. It is almost a certainty that killing of the entire family was the object of the negro. Sheriff Raley and posse have been in pursuit of the negro all day and have a clue which may lead to his arrest in a few hours. No doubt could the citizens of Crossley's neighborhood get possession of the negro before the Sheriff lands him in jail, he will be summarily dealt with.
tom-fifer-brewton-1903-08-24.A3:
ALLEGED POISONER CAUGHT.
Lee Pfeiffer, Charged with Dastardly Offense, Arrested.
Brewton, Aug. 26.—(Special.)—The negro, Lee Pfeiffer, who, at an early hour Monday morning made a diabolical attempt at poisoning the family of Matthew Crossley, near here, was arrested yesterday afternoon by Sheriff James W. Raley and posse at Tensaw River Railroad bridge, about fourteen miles this side of Mobile. Raley had been close upon the trail of the negro since Monday evening and yesterday his efforts to capture the criminal were rewarded.

All south-bound trains were searched, but the local freight did not stop at Hurricane Station. So the train was flagged on the trestle by the bridge tender and others, and it happened that the much-wanted man was on the train. With no avenue of escape, the negro was quickly covered and in the hands of an officer. He was brought to Brewton last night and lodged behind prison bars. He has been positively identified as the assailant of Crossley with a stone, and undoubtedly the man who put strychnine in a bucket of water, with the hope that the entire Crossley family would die.

Mr. Crossley was in town today and has two ugly wounds, one on his head and the other on his breast, inflicted by the young negro. Feeling runs high in the neighborhood of Crossley, and strong guard will be placed around the county

Negro Whips White Woman.
Negro Whips White Woman.

Washington, Pa., Aug. 19.—Mrs. Mary E. Myers, of Bunola, near Washington, was attacked and horsewhipped by a negro, W. S. Sanders, Monday afternoon. The woman was badly injured, and the negro is held for a trial at Court. Last Monday a large crowd of people gathered at the Monongahela wharf at Bunola, where a show boat was moored. Among the crowd were Mrs. Myers and her little daughter, and the negro Sanders, who is a teamster. The little Myers girl started a conversation with Sanders, when her mother reproved her, telling her to go away from the negro. This so enraged Sanders that, raising the heavy whip which he carried, he attacked Mrs. Myers, lashing her repeatedly about the face and body. The woman screamed with pain and fright and swooned. A rush was made for Sanders by bystanders, and he was dragged down the street by his legs. Cries of "Lynch him!" were heard on every side, and it was feared that the negro would be summarily dealt with. Officers, however, rescued him from the crowd and placed him in the borough prison. He was given a hearing, pleaded guilty and was remanded to the county jail to wait trial at Court. Mrs. Myers was so badly injured that she was unable to appear against him.

MASKED MEN
Hold Up Train, But Passengers Not Molested.
Search Made for Negro Who Shot Foreman of Construction Crew At Baker's Hill Tunnel.
About twenty masked men held up L. & N. train No. 51, which leaves here at 5:18 p. m., at the railroad construction camp near Ridgetop, Tenn., Saturday night. The men are supposed to have been in search of the negro. Will Reed, who shot and probably fatally wounded Ollie Ware, one of the foremen superintending the construction of the Louisville and Nashville railroad tunnel through Baker's Hill early Saturday morning.

Most of them carried rifles, and they were very quiet in their work. The men boarded the train and passed through all the coaches, scanning the passengers. They had handkerchiefs tied over their faces, concealing their features up to their eyes.

After going through the train they left as quietly as they had boarded, and it proceeded to Nashville, being delayed only a few minutes by the hold-up.

The negro wanted had been arrested a few miles east of Spring field. Officers made the trip to Nashville in a buggy. It was very fortunate for Reed that he was not put on the train, as the masked men would in all probability have made short work of him had he been a passenger.
will-reed-ridgetop-1903-08-29.A3:
HELD UP A TRAIN.
Fifteen or Twenty Masked Men in Search of Supt. Ware's Slayer. Nashville. Tenn. Aug. 29.-Fifteen
Search of Supt. Ware's Slayer.
Nashville, Tenn., Aug. 29.—Fifteen or twenty masked men held up the Louisville & Nashville passenger train due here at 8:25 at Ridgetop Station tonight in search for the negro, Will Reed, who shot Superintendent Ware of the Mason-Hogue Company, at Baker's Station today. The maskers signaled the engineer to stop and he did so. Then they boarded the train, and passing through each coach, carefully scrutinized every passenger. They failed to find their man.
will-reed-ridgetop-1903-08-29.A5:
LOUISA MAN MURDERED
Killed Near Nashville by a Negro Whom He Discharged.
(Special to the James-Dispatch.)

IRWIN, VA., Sept. 2.—The body of Mr. Ollie Ware, of Louisa county, was brought home last night from Nashville, Tenn., where he died. Mr. Ware was killed by a negro last Saturday morning and died the same evening. He was in charge of a number of negroes who were at work on a railroad in Tennessee, and was killed by a negro whom he had discharged. Mr. Ware was very popular with his employers, and had made many friends. He was quiet, sober and industrious, and had the confidence of every one who knew him.

The negro murderer was caught the same evening the crime was committed and was lodged in Nashville jail.

The matter caused a great deal of excitement in Nashville, and the negro will have a speedy trial.

william-bradway-salem-1903-08-26.A1:
A JEALOUS LOVER USES RAZOR ON RIVAL A Too Ardent Salem Colored Youth, Disappointed in Securing the Affection of a Young Girl, Slashes Her and His Rival with a Razor--Detective Carney Hunts Him and Runs the Would-be Murderer Down, and Lands Him in Jail
A colored youth by the name of William Bradway was given a hearing in Justice Smith's court, at Salem, on Wednesday, on a charge of murderously assaulting Spencer Seibert and Laura Doran, both colored, in Salem, on Sunday evening, August 16th.

A camp meeting was in progress in the rear of the Mt. Pisgah A. M. E. Church, on East Broadway, Salem, and it appears that the young man went to the mother of the girl and asked if he might take Laura to the meeting. The mother at once asked who he was, and, upon learning his name, refused his request. This angered him, and that night he hid himself in a dark place near where he thought Laura and her lover, Spencer Seibert, would pass. When they came along, he jumped from his hiding, pulled off his coat and began to flourish a razor, making a dash at Seibert and at the same time threatening that he would rip the black heart out of him. Seibert dodged to escape the blow, when he received an ugly gash, extending from his left ear to the top of his right eye. Bradway then made a slash at Miss Doran, and cut the muscle of her arm nearly through to the bone. This seemed to appease his wrath, and he quickly made his escape.

The injured persons managed to get to their home, when Dr. Carpenter was summoned, who dressed their wounds.

Bradway, it has been learned, went to Claysville, where he visited "Mouse" Robinson and requested the loan of a hat. Robinson went up stairs to secure one, and when he returned he found that Bradway had left and taken with him a revolver which he (Robinson) had just hired of Paul Erhardt. A search was made in Claysville but he could not be found.

The authorities were at once notified and Detective Carney was placed in charge of the case. While officiating at the race track a small boy informed the Detective that he had seen Bradway in the neighborhood of Quinton. The Detective, accompanied by the Sheriff and Chief of Police, journeyed out in that direction and espied the criminal in a corn field near William Carpenter's farm on the Quinton road. The Detective, pulling his revolver from his pocket, called for Bradway to halt, but the latter took to his feet and entered the barn on the Carpenter farm. He went to the mow and covered himself with the hay. The Chief, by jabbing a pitch fork in the hay, struck Bradway on the arm and he then readily gave up.

Bradway is a very dangerous character. He is now under bail to appear before the Cumberland County Courts to answer to the charge of attempted murder on an old lady near Bridgeton. It is claimed that he in company with other negroes went to the home of the old lady, and digging a hole in front of the door, informed her that they had come to kill and bury her. Her screams brought the assistance of neighbors before the crime could be committed.

It is said that he was sent to the Reform School from this county some years ago for larceny.

On Wednesday night when the officers were bringing Bradway through the upper part of the city, a mob of about three hundred people gathered about the wagon and tried to get hold of the prisoner, claiming that they wanted to lynch him.

HAPPENINGS IN ILLINOIS CITIES AND TOWNS. ALDERMAN PREVENTS NEGRO'S LYNCHING Frank Holten Drives Away With Intended Victim in Face of Angry Mob. CHASE ON WHISKY CHUTE. Posse With Ropes Chases William Hickson, Who Finally Is Locked in Police Station.
Alderman Frank Holten of East St. Louis last night saved William Hickson, an intoxicated negro, from lynching at the hands of an angry mob of blacks and whites on Whisky Chute, and brought the negro to the police station, where he was locked up.

Hickson had been drinking heavily early in the evening and he became imbued with the idea that some one was trying to injure him. He secured a revolver and flourished it in several places on Whisky Chute, chasing crowds of men and women out of stores and saloons.

The residents of Whisky Chute do not usually call in the services of policemen to keep the peace, but take the law in their own hands. A posse was organized, a rope was secured and the crowd started after the negro, chasing him several blocks. It was said that several shots were fired, when Alderman Holten happened along. He was driving and inquired into the cause of the excitement. It was told him and he managed to catch the negro, whom he placed in his rig, and with the assistance of Roundsman Paddy Ryan, who arrived in the meantime, stood off the mob and took the negro to the police station.

Sault Ste Marie, Mich., Sept. 15.—A fire which originated in Klosser's candy store here tonight, and which is still burning, has destroyed an entire block of stores in the heart of the business district. The damage already done amounts to about $100,000.

The principal losers are H. L. Newton, who owns most of the business buildings destroyed, and D. K. Moses & Son, proprietors of the largest department store in the city.

Kansas City, Sept. 15.—Martin Duffy knocked out Philadelphia Tommy Ryan in the eighth round of a slow and uninteresting fight. Many of the spectators left the hall in disgust after the fight had gone a few rounds.

LYNCHED ON STREET.

Negro Strnng Up by a Mob of Irate Mississippi.

SEEKING LABORERS.

Had a Quarrel With a White Man in Regard to Inducing Negroes to Leave Centerville and Latter Killed.
Houston, Sept. 16.—A Post special from Centerville, Miss., says: William Williams, a negro, was lynched on Main street of Centerville by a mob of several hundred people. Williams, who was a laboring agent, has been here several days employing negroes for contractors in other sections of the state. It is alleged that he enticed several employees of the Robinson Mercantile company to leave that concern, and James H. Germany, a white employee of the Robinson company, met him on the street and remonstrated with him about his conduct. A quarrel followed and Williams drew a revolver and shot Germany dead.

The negro attempted to escape after killing Germany, but a mob was quickly on his heels and a running fight followed, which ended in the negro being captured and shot to death by the crowd.
william-williams-centerville-1903-09-15.A13:
NEGRO MURDERER SHOT DOWN. He Was a Labor Agent and Had Killed a White Man in a Row.
NEW ORLEANS, Sept. 16.—James H. Germany, a manager of the Robinson Mercantile Company of Centreville, Miss., was murdered yesterday by a negro named Will Williams, who was killed soon afterward.

Williams was a labor agent and had persuaded several of the hands employed by the Robinson company to break their contracts. When Germany warned him that this was ruinous and had to be stopped, Williams drew his revolver and fired three shots, the first of which passed through Germany's heart.

The killing occurred on Main street, in front of the Robinson store. The discharge of the pistol brought a crowd at once and Williams was chased down the street. He fired as he ran, emptying his pistol several times, but was brought down by a volley of bullets just at the town line.

Rapid Action.
At Centerville last week James H. Germany, an employee of the Robinson Mercantile Company, was killed by a negro named Williams. The negro had been enticing the labor of the company away, and was approached on the matter by Mr. Germany, when he pulled his pistol and fired three shots at Mr. Germany at close range. The first shot produced instant death. The negro was chased down the streets, but owing to the crowd of people attracted by the shooting no one dared to use a gun. As soon as Williams left Main street a general melee began, Williams returning the fire of the crowd as he ran off. He was overtaken before getting out of the town limits, and his body riddled with bullets. Williams showed poor marksmanship, or he would have killed several persons. He emptied his pistol several times at the crowd at close range while dodging behind trees and other objects. Everything is quiet and no further trouble is anticipated. Mr. Germany leaves a wife and five children and a host of friends.

HOBOES ARE IN CAMP
And They Don't Seem to Make Neighbors That Frankfort Is in Love With.
ENGLE'S SHORTAGE CONFIRMED
Put at About $30,000 and Suicide Probable-Litigation Over a Dam Site-State Notes.
Frankfort, Ind., Nov. 2. — Hoboes have established a permanent camp in the western outskirts of this city, the tramps' retreat being located near the Clover Leaf right-of-way. Nightly from twenty-five to fifty of these human drones assemble there and indulge in disgraceful orgies. Now that the nights are becoming cold, the tramps are doing damage by stealing and burning valuable timber, the Clover Leaf railroad being one of the greatest sufferers in this respect, as the vagabonds appropriate bridge timbers, etc. All of the residences on the west side are visited daily by tramps, and the large pile of chicken feathers in the vicinity of the camp proves very plainly the fate of chickens that have been missed by poultry owners. It is probable that the Clover Leaf Railroad company and the local authorities will unite in a vigorous campaign on this camp, in the hope of abolishing it.

Drove a Negro Into the River.

Muncie, Ind., Nov. 2.—Colored men are unpopular in the village Yorktown, six miles west of here, and when a negro was seen prowling around the place in a suspicious manner a mob of twenty-five of the "best citizens" started in pursuit of him. The colored man refused to heed the command to halt and, with the mob at his heels, hurried away, finally escaping by jumping into the river and swimming to the other side.

They Had Reason, You Bet.

Greencastle, Ind., Nov. 2. — After perforating the doors of the safe in the Vandalia freight office here and loading them with nitro-glycerine would-be burglars left for some unknown reason. There was a large amount of money, which was not molested, the charge having been allowed to remain unexploded.

Engle Was $30,000 Short.

Vincennes, Ind., Nov. 2.—J. J. Murphy, secretary of the Vincennes Distilling company, verifies the report that the late W. H. Engle, treasurer of the company, is short in his accounts with the company. The amount is placed at $30,000. Experts are at work on the books. Murphy thinks Engle killed himself.
